translation:
K. stared at the guard. Was he meant to receive lessons from a possibly younger man? Was he being reprimanded for his openness? And he was getting no information about the reason for his arrest or who had ordered it? He became agitated, paced back and forth, unhindered by anyone, pushed back his cuffs, felt his chest, smoothed his hair, passed the three gentlemen and said, "It's pointless," upon which they turned to him, looking at him with a friendly but serious expression, and finally stopped in front of the guard's table again.

"Prosecutor Hasterer is a good friend of mine," he said, "can I telephone him?"

"Certainly," said the guard, "but I don't see what sense that would serve, unless you have some private matter to discuss with him."

"What sense?" cried K., more startled than annoyed. "Who are you? You want a sense, and you're staging the most pointless thing there is? Isn't it absurd? The gentlemen first attacked me, and now they're sitting or standing here and letting me lecture you all. What sense would there be in telephoning a prosecutor when I'm supposedly arrested? Well, I won't telephone."

"But please do," said the guard and stretched out his hand towards the next room where the telephone was, "please, telephone."

"No, I won't," said K. and went to the window. Across the way the society was still at the window and seemed only now, by K.'s approaching the window, to be slightly disturbed in its quiet observation. The older men wanted to get up, but the man behind them calmed them down.

"Look, there are also such spectators!" cried K. loudly to the guard and pointed with his finger outwards. "Away from there!" he then called over there. The three retreated a few steps at once, the two old men even behind the man who covered them with his broad body and, judging by his mouth movements, was saying something incomprehensible at a distance. They didn't disappear completely, though, but seemed to be waiting for the moment when they could approach the window again unnoticed.

"Nosy, inconsiderate people!" said K. as he turned back into the room. The guard possibly agreed, as K. thought with a side glance. But it was just as well possible that he hadn't even listened, for he had a hand firmly pressed on the table and seemed to be comparing the length of his fingers. The two guards sat on a chest covered with a decorative cloth and rubbed their knees. The three young men had their hands on their hips and looked aimlessly around. It was as quiet as in some forgotten office.

"Well, gentlemen," cried K., it seemed to him for a moment as if he were carrying them all on his shoulders, "judging by your appearance, my affair must be finished. I think it's best not to think any more about the justification or lack of justification of your actions and to bring a conciliatory end to the matter with a handshake. If you agree with me, then please—" and he walked to the guard's table and held out his hand.

The guard raised his eyes, gnawed on his lips and looked at K.'s outstretched hand; K. still believed that the guard would strike. However, the guard stood up, took a hard, round hat that was lying on Miss Bürstner's bed, and carefully placed it on his head with both hands, as one does when trying on a new hat.

"How easy things seem to you!" he said to K. "We should bring a conciliatory end to the matter, did you say? No, no, that really won't do. With which, I certainly don't mean to say that you should despair. No, why should you? You're only arrested, that's all. I told you that, I did, and I also saw how you took it. That's enough for today, and we can say goodbye, though only provisionally. You'll probably want to go to the bank now?"

"To the bank?" asked K., "I thought I was arrested."

K. asked with a certain defiance, for although his handshake hadn't been accepted, he felt, particularly since the guard had stood up, increasingly independent of all these people. He was playing with them. He had the intention, if they were to go away, to run after them to the front door and offer them his arrest. Therefore, he repeated: "How can I go to the bank when I'm arrested?"

"Ah, so," said the guard, who was already at the door, "you misunderstood me. You are arrested, yes, but that shouldn't prevent you from fulfilling your duties. Your usual way of life shouldn't be hindered either."

"Then being arrested isn't so bad," said K. and came closer to the guard.

"I never meant it any other way," said the latter.

"But it doesn't even seem necessary to have communicated the arrest," said K. and came even closer. All of them had also moved closer. Now they were all gathered in a confined space at the door.

"It was my duty," said the guard.

"A stupid duty," said K. stubbornly.

"Perhaps," answered the guard, "but we won't waste our time with such talk. I assumed you wanted to go to the bank. Since you're paying attention to every word, I'll add: I'm not forcing you to go to the bank, I just assumed you wanted to. And to make it easier for you and to make your arrival at the bank as inconspicuous as possible, I had these three gentlemen, your colleagues, at your disposal."

"What?" exclaimed K. and stared at the three. These such uncharacteristic, pale, young men, whom he still only remembered from photographs in a group, were actually officials from his bank, not colleagues, that was too much said and proved a gap in the all-knowledge of the guard, but subordinate officials from the bank they were. How had K. overlooked this? How had he had to put up with it from the guard and the guards to not recognize these three! The stiff, swinging Rabensteiner, the blonde Kullich with his deep-set eyes and Kaminer with the unbearable, chronically muscle-strained smile.

"Good morning!" said K. after a while and shook the hands of the gentlemen, who bowed correctly. "I didn't recognize you at all. Well, then, shall we go to work?"

The gentlemen nodded, laughing and eagerly, as if they had been waiting for just this moment. But just as K. missed his hat, which was lying in his room, they all ran after it one after the other, which at least suggested a certain awkwardness. K. stood still and watched them through the two open doors, the last one, of course, being the indifferent Rabensteiner, who had just taken an elegant trot. Kaminer handed over the hat, and K. had to say, as was often necessary at the bank, expressly that Kaminer's smile was not intentional, that he couldn't actually smile on purpose. In the anteroom, Frau Grubach, who didn't look very guilty, opened the front door to the whole company, and K. saw, as so often, down on her apron band, which cut so unnecessarily deep into her powerful body.

Downstairs, K. decided, with the clock in his hand, to take a car to avoid increasing the already half-hour delay. Kaminer ran to the corner to fetch the car, the other two apparently tried to distract K. when suddenly Kullich pointed to the opposite gate, in which the tall man with the blond pointed beard appeared and, at first a little embarrassed about now showing himself in his full size, retreated to the wall and leaned against it. The old men were probably still on the stairs. K. was annoyed with Kullich for pointing out the man, whom he had already seen earlier, indeed whom he had even expected.

"Don't look!" he blurted out, without noticing how conspicuous such a way of speaking was towards independent men. But it wasn't even necessary to explain, because just then the car arrived, they got in and drove off. Then K. remembered that he hadn't noticed the guard and the guards leaving at all, the guard had concealed the three officials from him and now the officials the guard. That didn't show much quick thinking, and K. decided to observe himself in this regard more closely. But he involuntarily turned back and bent over the back of the car to possibly see the guard and the guards again. But immediately turned back and leaned comfortably in the corner of the car, without even trying to look for anyone. Although it didn't seem like it, he would have needed support right now, but now the gentlemen seemed tired, Rabensteiner was looking to the right out of the car, Kullich to the left, and only Kaminer was standing with his grin available, over which humanity unfortunately forbade making a joke.
source_text: K. starrte den Aufseher an. Schulmäßige Lehren bekam er hier von einem vielleicht jüngeren Menschen? Für seine Offenheit wurde er mit einer Rüge bestraft? Und über den Grund seiner Verhaftung und über deren Auftraggeber erfuhr er nichts? Er geriet in eine gewisse Aufregung, ging auf und ab, woran ihn niemand hinderte, schob seine Manschetten zurück, befühlte die Brust, strich sein Haar zurecht, kam an den drei Herren vorüber, sagte: »Es ist ja sinnlos«, worauf sich diese zu ihm umdrehten und ihn entgegenkommend, aber ernst ansahen und machte endlich wieder vor dem Tisch des Aufsehers halt. »Der Staatsanwalt Hasterer ist mein guter Freund«, sagte er, »kann ich ihm telephonieren?« »Gewiß«, sagte der Aufseher, »aber ich weiß nicht, welchen Sinn das haben sollte, es müßte denn sein, daß Sie irgendeine private Angelegenheit mit ihm zu besprechen haben.« »Welchen Sinn?« rief K., mehr bestürzt als geärgert. »Wer sind Sie denn? Sie wollen einen Sinn und führen das Sinnloseste auf, das es gibt? Ist es nicht zum Steinerweichen? Die Herren haben mich zuerst überfallen, und jetzt sitzen oder stehen sie hier herum und lassen mich vor Ihnen die Hohe Schule reiten. Welchen Sinn es hätte, an einen Staatsanwalt zu telephonieren, wenn ich angeblich verhaftet bin? Gut, ich werde nicht telephonieren.« »Aber doch«, sagte der Aufseher und streckte die Hand zum Vorzimmer aus, wo das Telephon war, »bitte, telephonieren Sie doch.« »Nein, ich will nicht mehr«, sagte K. und ging zum Fenster. Drüben war noch die Gesellschaft beim Fenster und schien nur jetzt dadurch, daß K. ans Fenster herangetreten war, in der Ruhe des Zuschauens ein wenig gestört. Die Alten wollten sich erheben, aber der Mann hinter ihnen beruhigte sie. »Dort sind auch solche Zuschauer«, rief K. ganz laut dem Aufseher zu und zeigte mit dem Zeigefinger hinaus. »Weg von dort«, rief er dann hinüber. Die drei wichen auch sofort ein paar Schritte zurück, die beiden Alten sogar noch hinter den Mann, der sie mit seinem breiten Körper deckte und, nach seinen Mundbewegungen zu schließen, irgend etwas auf die Entfernung hin Unverständliches sagte. Ganz aber verschwanden sie nicht, sondern schienen auf den Augenblick zu warten, in dem sie sich unbemerkt wieder dem Fenster nähern könnten. »Zudringliche, rücksichtslose Leute!« sagte K., als er sich ins Zimmer zurückwendete. Der Aufseher stimmte ihm möglicherweise zu, wie K. mit einem Seitenblick zu erkennen glaubte. Aber es war ebensogut möglich, daß er gar nicht zugehört hatte, denn er hatte eine Hand fest auf den Tisch gedrückt und schien die Finger ihrer Länge nach zu vergleichen. Die zwei Wächter saßen auf einem mit einer Schmuckdecke verhüllten Koffer und rieben ihre Knie. Die drei jungen Leute hatten die Hände in die Hüften gelegt und sahen ziellos herum. Es war still wie in irgendeinem vergessenen Büro. »Nun, meine Herren«, rief K., es schien ihm einen Augenblick lang, als trage er alle auf seinen Schultern, »Ihrem Aussehen nach zu schließen, dürfte meine Angelegenheit beendet sein. Ich bin der Ansicht, daß es am besten ist, über die Berechtigung oder Nichtberechtigung Ihres Vorgehens nicht mehr nachzudenken und der Sache durch einen gegenseitigen Händedruck einen versöhnlichen Abschluß zu geben. Wenn auch Sie meiner Ansicht sind, dann bitte –« und er trat an den Tisch des Aufsehers hin und reichte ihm die Hand. Der Aufseher hob die Augen, nagte an den Lippen und sah auf K.s ausgestreckte Hand; noch immer glaubte K., der Aufseher werde einschlagen. Dieser aber stand auf, nahm einen harten, runden Hut, der auf Fräulein Bürstners Bett lag, und setzte sich ihn vorsichtig mit beiden Händen auf, wie man es bei der Anprobe neuer Hüte tut. »Wie einfach Ihnen alles scheint!« sagte er dabei zu K. »wir sollten der Sache einen versöhnlichen Abschluß geben, meinten Sie? Nein, nein, das geht wirklich nicht. Womit ich andererseits durchaus nicht sagen will, daß Sie verzweifeln sollen. Nein, warum denn? Sie sind nur verhaftet, nichts weiter. Das hatte ich Ihnen mitzuteilen, habe es getan und habe auch gesehen, wie Sie es aufgenommen haben. Damit ist es für heute genug und wir können uns verabschieden, allerdings nur vorläufig. Sie werden wohl jetzt in die Bank gehen wollen?« »In die Bank?« fragte K., »ich dachte, ich wäre verhaftet.« K. fragte mit einem gewissen Trotz, denn obwohl sein Handschlag nicht angenommen worden war, fühlte er sich, insbesondere seitdem der Aufseher aufgestanden war, immer unabhängiger von allen diesen Leuten. Er spielte mit ihnen. Er hatte die Absicht, falls sie weggehen sollten, bis zum Haustor nachzulaufen und ihnen seine Verhaftung anzubieten. Darum wiederholte er auch: »Wie kann ich denn in die Bank gehen, da ich verhaftet bin?« »Ach so«, sagte der Aufseher, der schon bei der Tür war, »Sie haben mich mißverstanden. Sie sind verhaftet, gewiß, aber das soll Sie nicht hindern, Ihren Beruf zu erfüllen. Sie sollen auch Ihrer gewöhnlichen Lebensweise nicht gehindert sein.« »Dann ist das Verhaftetsein nicht sehr schlimm«, sagte K. und ging nahe an den Aufseher heran. »Ich meinte es niemals anders«, sagte dieser. »Es scheint aber dann nicht einmal die Mitteilung der Verhaftung sehr notwendig gewesen zu sein«, sagte K. und ging noch näher. Auch die anderen hatten sich genähert. Alle waren jetzt auf einem engen Raum bei der Tür versammelt. »Es war meine Pflicht«, sagte der Aufseher. »Eine dumme Pflicht«, sagte K. unnachgiebig. »Mag sein«, antwortete der Aufseher, »aber wir wollen mit solchen Reden nicht unsere Zeit verlieren. Ich hatte angenommen, daß Sie in die Bank gehen wollen. Da Sie auf alle Worte aufpassen, füge ich hinzu: ich zwinge Sie nicht, in die Bank zu gehen, ich hatte nur angenommen, daß Sie es wollen. Und um Ihnen das zu erleichtern und Ihre Ankunft in der Bank möglichst unauffällig zu machen, habe ich diese drei Herren, Ihre Kollegen, hier zu Ihrer Verfügung gehalten.« »Wie?« rief K. und staunte die drei an. Diese so uncharakteristischen, blutarmen, jungen Leute, die er immer noch nur als Gruppe bei den Photographien in der Erinnerung hatte, waren tatsächlich Beamte aus seiner Bank, nicht Kollegen, das war zu viel gesagt und bewies eine Lücke in der Allwissenheit des Aufsehers, aber untergeordnete Beamte aus der Bank waren es allerdings. Wie hatte K. das übersehen können? Wie hatte er doch hingenommen sein müssen von dem Aufseher und den Wächtern, um diese drei nicht zu erkennen! Den steifen, die Hände schwingenden Rabensteiner, den blonden Kullich mit den tiefliegenden Augen und Kaminer mit dem unausstehlichen, durch eine chronische Muskelzerrung bewirkten Lächeln. »Guten Morgen!« sagte K. nach einem Weilchen und reichte den sich korrekt verbeugenden Herren die Hand. »Ich habe Sie gar nicht erkannt. Nun werden wir also an die Arbeit gehen, nicht?« Die Herren nickten lachend und eifrig, als hätten sie die ganze Zeit über darauf gewartet, nur als K. seinen Hut vermißte, der in seinem Zimmer liegengeblieben war, liefen sie sämtlich hintereinander, ihn holen, was immerhin auf eine gewisse Verlegenheit schließen ließ. K. stand still und sah ihnen durch die zwei offenen Türen nach, der letzte war natürlich der gleichgültige Rabensteiner, der bloß einen eleganten Trab angeschlagen hatte. Kaminer überreichte den Hut, und K. mußte sich, wie dies übrigens auch öfters in der Bank nötig war, ausdrücklich sagen, daß Kaminers Lächeln nicht Absicht war, ja daß er überhaupt absichtlich nicht lächeln konnte. Im Vorzimmer öffnete dann Frau Grubach, die gar nicht sehr schuldbewußt aussah, der ganzen Gesellschaft die Wohnungstür, und K. sah, wie so oft, auf ihr Schürzenband nieder, das so unnötig tief in ihren mächtigen Leib einschnitt. Unten entschloß sich K., die Uhr in der Hand, ein Automobil zu nehmen, um die schon halbstündige Verspätung nicht unnötig zu vergrößern. Kaminer lief zur Ecke, um den Wagen zu holen, die zwei anderen versuchten offensichtlich, K. zu zerstreuen, als plötzlich Kullich auf das gegenüberliegende Haustor zeigte, in dem eben der große Mann mit dem blonden Spitzbart erschien und, im ersten Augenblick ein wenig verlegen darüber, daß er sich jetzt in seiner ganzen Größe zeigte, zur Wand zurücktrat und sich anlehnte. Die Alten waren wohl noch auf der Treppe. K. ärgerte sich über Kullich, daß dieser auf den Mann aufmerksam machte, den er selbst schon früher gesehen, ja den er sogar erwartet hatte. »Schauen Sie nicht hin!« stieß er hervor, ohne zu bemerken, wie auffallend eine solche Redeweise gegenüber selbständigen Männern war. Es war aber auch keine Erklärung nötig, denn gerade kam das Automobil, man setzte sich und fuhr los. Da erinnerte sich K., daß er das Weggehen des Aufsehers und der Wächter gar nicht bemerkt hatte, der Aufseher hatte ihm die drei Beamten verdeckt und nun wieder die Beamten den Aufseher. Viel Geistesgegenwart bewies das nicht, und K. nahm sich vor, sich in dieser Hinsicht genauer zu beobachten. Doch drehte er sich noch unwillkürlich um und beugte sich über das Hinterdeck des Automobils vor, um möglicherweise den Aufseher und die Wächter noch zu sehen. Aber gleich wendete er sich wieder zurück und lehnte sich bequem in die Wagenecke, ohne auch nur den Versuch gemacht zu haben, jemanden zu suchen. Obwohl es nicht den Anschein hatte, hätte er gerade jetzt Zuspruch nötig gehabt, aber nun schienen die Herren ermüdet, Rabensteiner sah rechts aus dem Wagen, Kullich links, und nur Kaminer stand mit seinem Grinsen zur Verfügung, über das einen Spaß zu machen leider die Menschlichkeit verbot.

And to learn nothing about why he had been arrested and on whose orders? He grew increasingly agitated, paced up and down, freely and without hindrance, pushed his cuffs back, felt his chest, brushed his hair into place, went past the three men, muttering, “It’s completely senseless,” at which they turned and looked at him in a friendly but serious way, and finally came to a stop before the inspector’s table. “Hasterer, the public prosecutor, is a good friend of mine,” he said, “can I telephone him?” “Certainly,” said the inspector, “but I don’t see what sense it makes, unless you have some private matter to discuss with him.” “What sense?” K. cried out, more startled than annoyed. “Who do you think you are? You ask what sense it makes, while you stage the most senseless performance imaginable? Wouldn’t it break a heart of stone? First these gentlemen assault me, and now they sit around or stand about and put me through my paces before you. What sense is there in telephoning a lawyer when I’ve supposedly been arrested? Fine, I won’t telephone.” “But do,” said the inspector, and waved toward the hall, where the telephone was, “please do telephone.” “No, I no longer wish to,” K. said, and went to the window. Across the way the group was still at the window, their peaceful observation now slightly disturbed as K. stepped to the window. The old couple started to rise, but the man behind them calmed them down. “There’s more of the audience over there,” K. cried out to the inspector and pointed outside. “Get away from there,” he yelled at them. The three immediately retreated a few steps, the old couple even withdrawing behind the man, who shielded them with his broad body and, judging by the movement of his lips, apparently said something that couldn’t be understood at that distance. They didn’t disappear entirely, however, but instead seemed to wait for the moment when they could approach the window again unnoticed. “Obnoxious, thoughtless people!” said K., turning back to the room. The inspector may have agreed with him, as he thought he noticed with a sideways glance. You ask me to be sensible and you carry on in the most senseless way imaginable yourself! It's enough to sicken the dogs. People first fall upon me in my own house and then lounge about the room and put me through my paces for your benefit. What sense would there be in telephoning to a lawyer when I'm supposed to be under arrest? All right, I won't telephone." Kaminer ran to the corner to summon it, and the two others were making obvious efforts to keep K. diverted when Kullich pointed to the doorway of the house on the other side of the street where the large man with the blonde goatee beard appeared and, a little embarrassed at first at letting himself be seen in his full height, stepped back to the wall and leant against it. The old couple were probably still on the stairs. K. was cross with Kullich for pointing out this man whom he had already seen himself, in fact whom he had been expecting. " Don't look at him!" he snapped, without noticing how odd it was to speak to free men in this way. But there was no explanation needed anyway as just then the taxi arrived, they sat inside and set off. Inside the taxi, K. remembered that he had not noticed the supervisor and the policemen leaving - the supervisor had stopped him noticing the three bank staff and now the three bank staff had stopped him noticing the supervisor. This showed that K. was not very attentive, and he resolved to watch himself more carefully in this respect. Nonetheless, he gave it no thought as he twisted himself round and leant over onto the rear shelf of the car to catch sight of the supervisor and the policemen if he could. But he turned back round straight away and leant comfortably into the corner of the taxi without even having made the effort to see anyone. Although it did not seem like it, now was just the time when he needed some encouragement, but the gentlemen seemed tired just then, Rabensteiner looked out of the car to the right, Kullich to the left and only Kaminer was there with his grin at K.'s service. It would have been inhumane to make fun of that.

translation: K. stared at the warden. Was he meant to learn obedience from someone younger than himself? Was he being reprimanded for his openness? And he hadn't even been told the reason for his arrest, or who had ordered it? He felt a surge of agitation, paced back and forth, unhindered by anyone, pushed back his cuffs, touched his chest, smoothed his hair, and passed the three gentlemen, saying, "It's pointless," whereupon they turned to face him, appearing both conciliatory and serious. He finally stopped before the warden's table. "Prosecutor Hasterer is a good friend of mine," he said, "can I make a phone call to him?" "Certainly," said the warden, "but I don't see what sense that would make, unless you have some private matter to discuss with him." "What sense?" exclaimed K., more astonished than annoyed. "Who are you? You want a sense, and you're enacting the most pointless thing imaginable. Isn't it ridiculous? The gentlemen first ambushed me, and now they're just sitting or standing here, letting me give them a lecture. What sense would there be in calling a prosecutor if I'm supposedly arrested? Well, I won't be calling." "But do," said the warden, and extended his hand towards the anteroom where the telephone was, "please, make the call." "No, I won't," said K., and walked towards the window. Across the way, the company was still by the window, and only seemed disturbed by K.'s approach, breaking their quiet observation. The older men tried to rise, but the man behind them calmed them down. "There are spectators over there too!" shouted K. loudly at the warden, and pointed with his finger. "Away from there!" he then called across. The three retreated a few steps immediately, the two older ones even behind the man who covered them with his broad frame and, judging by his mouth movements, was saying something unintelligible in the distance. But they didn't entirely disappear, but seemed to be waiting for the moment they could approach the window unnoticed again. "Insolent, inconsiderate people!" said K., as he turned back into the room. The warden possibly agreed, as K. believed, catching a glimpse of him from the corner of his eye. But it was just as well possible that he hadn't been listening, because he had a hand firmly pressed on the table, seemingly comparing the length of his fingers. The two guards were sitting on a trunk covered with a decorative cloth, rubbing their knees. The three young men had their hands on their hips and looked around aimlessly. It was as silent as in some forgotten office. "Well, gentlemen," said K., it seemed to him for a moment as if he were carrying the weight of everything on his shoulders, "judging by your appearance, my matter must be finished. I believe it's best not to dwell on the justification or lack thereof for your actions and to bring a conciliatory conclusion to the matter with a handshake. If you agree, then please —" and he stepped towards the warden's table and offered his hand. The warden lifted his eyes, gnawed his lips, and looked at K.'s outstretched hand; K. still believed the warden would strike. But instead, the warden stood up, took a stiff, round hat which was lying on Miss Bürstner's bed, and carefully put it on his head with both hands, as one does when trying on a new hat. "How simple things seem to you!" he said to K. "We should bring a conciliatory conclusion to the matter, did you say? No, no, that's really not possible. Although, I don't mean to say that you should despair. No, why should you? You are merely arrested, that's all. I told you that, I did, and I saw how you received it. That's enough for today, and we can say goodbye, although only temporarily. I suppose you'll be going to the bank now?" "To the bank?" asked K., "I thought I was arrested." K. asked with a certain defiance, because although his handshake hadn't been accepted, he felt, particularly since the warden had stood up, increasingly independent of all these people. He was playing with them. He intended, if they should leave, to run after them to the front door and offer them his arrest. So he repeated: "How can I go to the bank if I'm arrested?" "Oh so," said the warden, who was already by the door, "you misunderstood me. You are arrested, certainly, but that shouldn't prevent you from fulfilling your duties. It shouldn't hinder your usual way of life either." "Then being arrested isn't so bad," said K., and stepped closer to the warden. "I never meant it any other way," said the warden. "But it doesn't seem like the notification of the arrest was even necessary," said K., and stepped even closer. Everyone had gathered now in the narrow space by the door. "It was my duty," said the warden. "A foolish duty," said K., uncompromisingly. "Perhaps," replied the warden, "but we don't want to waste our time with such talk. I assumed you wanted to go to the bank. Since you pay attention to every word, I add: I'm not forcing you to go to the bank, I just assumed you would. And to make it easier for you and to make your arrival at the bank as inconspicuous as possible, I had these three gentlemen, your colleagues, at your disposal." "What?" exclaimed K., staring at the three. These so uncharacteristic, pale, young men, whom he still only remembered as a group in the photographs, were actually officials from his bank, not colleagues, that was an exaggeration, and proved a gap in the warden's omniscience, but they were indeed junior officials from the bank. How could K. have overlooked this? How had he had to put up with being ignored by the warden and the guards to not recognize these three? The stiff, swinging Rabensteiner, the blond Kullich with the deeply set eyes and Kaminer with the unbearable smile, caused by a chronic muscle spasm. "Good morning!" said K. after a while and offered the gentlemen, who bowed politely, his hand. "I didn't recognize you at all. Well then, we're going to work, aren't we?" The gentlemen nodded, laughing and eagerly, as if they had been waiting for this all along. Just as K.'s hat disappeared from his mind, they all ran after him to fetch it, which at least suggested a certain embarrassment. K. stood still and watched them through the two open doors, the last one, of course, being the indifferent Rabensteiner, who had simply struck an elegant trot. Kaminer handed K. his hat, and K. had to explicitly say, as was often necessary in the bank, that Kaminer's smile was not intentional, that he simply couldn't smile on purpose. In the anteroom, Mrs. Grubach, who didn't look very guilty, opened the apartment door for the whole company, and K. saw, as so often, the apron band pinned far too low on her stout body. Downstairs, K., with the watch in his hand, decided to take a car to avoid increasing the already half-hour delay. Kaminer went to the corner to fetch the car, the other two obviously tried to distract K., when suddenly Kullich pointed to the opposite gate, through which the tall man with the blond pointed beard appeared, stepping back slightly at first, embarrassed to be showing his full height, and leaning against the wall. The older men were probably still on the stairs. K. was annoyed with Kullich for pointing out the man whom he had already seen, and even expected. "Don't look!" he exclaimed, without noticing how unusual such a statement was towards independent men. But it wasn't necessary anyway, because the car just arrived, they got in and drove off. Then K. remembered that he hadn't even noticed the warden and the guards leaving, the warden had concealed the three officials, and now the officials had concealed the warden. This didn't show much presence of mind, and K. resolved to observe himself more closely in this regard. But he involuntarily turned back and leaned over the back of the car, trying to see the warden and the guards again. But then he turned back again and leaned comfortably into the corner of the car, without even attempting to look for anyone. Although he didn't seem to be in need of support, the gentlemen seemed tired, Rabensteiner looked right out of the car, Kullich left, and only Kaminer stood with his grin, which one was unfortunately forbidden to make fun of.
source_text: K. starrte den Aufseher an. Schulmäßige Lehren bekam er hier von einem vielleicht jüngeren Menschen? Für seine Offenheit wurde er mit einer Rüge bestraft? Und über den Grund seiner Verhaftung und über deren Auftraggeber erfuhr er nichts? Er geriet in eine gewisse Aufregung, ging auf und ab, woran ihn niemand hinderte, schob seine Manschetten zurück, befühlte die Brust, strich sein Haar zurecht, kam an den drei Herren vorüber, sagte: »Es ist ja sinnlos«, worauf sich diese zu ihm umdrehten und ihn entgegenkommend, aber ernst ansahen und machte endlich wieder vor dem Tisch des Aufsehers halt. »Der Staatsanwalt Hasterer ist mein guter Freund«, sagte er, »kann ich ihm telephonieren?« »Gewiß«, sagte der Aufseher, »aber ich weiß nicht, welchen Sinn das haben sollte, es müßte denn sein, daß Sie irgendeine private Angelegenheit mit ihm zu besprechen haben.« »Welchen Sinn?« rief K., mehr bestürzt als geärgert. »Wer sind Sie denn? Sie wollen einen Sinn und führen das Sinnloseste auf, das es gibt? Ist es nicht zum Steinerweichen? Die Herren haben mich zuerst überfallen, und jetzt sitzen oder stehen sie hier herum und lassen mich vor Ihnen die Hohe Schule reiten. Welchen Sinn es hätte, an einen Staatsanwalt zu telephonieren, wenn ich angeblich verhaftet bin? Gut, ich werde nicht telephonieren.« »Aber doch«, sagte der Aufseher und streckte die Hand zum Vorzimmer aus, wo das Telephon war, »bitte, telephonieren Sie doch.« »Nein, ich will nicht mehr«, sagte K. und ging zum Fenster. Drüben war noch die Gesellschaft beim Fenster und schien nur jetzt dadurch, daß K. ans Fenster herangetreten war, in der Ruhe des Zuschauens ein wenig gestört. Die Alten wollten sich erheben, aber der Mann hinter ihnen beruhigte sie. »Dort sind auch solche Zuschauer«, rief K. ganz laut dem Aufseher zu und zeigte mit dem Zeigefinger hinaus. »Weg von dort«, rief er dann hinüber. Die drei wichen auch sofort ein paar Schritte zurück, die beiden Alten sogar noch hinter den Mann, der sie mit seinem breiten Körper deckte und, nach seinen Mundbewegungen zu schließen, irgend etwas auf die Entfernung hin Unverständliches sagte. Ganz aber verschwanden sie nicht, sondern schienen auf den Augenblick zu warten, in dem sie sich unbemerkt wieder dem Fenster nähern könnten. »Zudringliche, rücksichtslose Leute!« sagte K., als er sich ins Zimmer zurückwendete. Der Aufseher stimmte ihm möglicherweise zu, wie K. mit einem Seitenblick zu erkennen glaubte. Aber es war ebensogut möglich, daß er gar nicht zugehört hatte, denn er hatte eine Hand fest auf den Tisch gedrückt und schien die Finger ihrer Länge nach zu vergleichen. Die zwei Wächter saßen auf einem mit einer Schmuckdecke verhüllten Koffer und rieben ihre Knie. Die drei jungen Leute hatten die Hände in die Hüften gelegt und sahen ziellos herum. Es war still wie in irgendeinem vergessenen Büro. »Nun, meine Herren«, rief K., es schien ihm einen Augenblick lang, als trage er alle auf seinen Schultern, »Ihrem Aussehen nach zu schließen, dürfte meine Angelegenheit beendet sein. Ich bin der Ansicht, daß es am besten ist, über die Berechtigung oder Nichtberechtigung Ihres Vorgehens nicht mehr nachzudenken und der Sache durch einen gegenseitigen Händedruck einen versöhnlichen Abschluß zu geben. Wenn auch Sie meiner Ansicht sind, dann bitte –« und er trat an den Tisch des Aufsehers hin und reichte ihm die Hand. Der Aufseher hob die Augen, nagte an den Lippen und sah auf K.s ausgestreckte Hand; noch immer glaubte K., der Aufseher werde einschlagen. Dieser aber stand auf, nahm einen harten, runden Hut, der auf Fräulein Bürstners Bett lag, und setzte sich ihn vorsichtig mit beiden Händen auf, wie man es bei der Anprobe neuer Hüte tut. »Wie einfach Ihnen alles scheint!« sagte er dabei zu K. »wir sollten der Sache einen versöhnlichen Abschluß geben, meinten Sie? Nein, nein, das geht wirklich nicht. Womit ich andererseits durchaus nicht sagen will, daß Sie verzweifeln sollen. Nein, warum denn? Sie sind nur verhaftet, nichts weiter. Das hatte ich Ihnen mitzuteilen, habe es getan und habe auch gesehen, wie Sie es aufgenommen haben. Damit ist es für heute genug und wir können uns verabschieden, allerdings nur vorläufig. Sie werden wohl jetzt in die Bank gehen wollen?« »In die Bank?« fragte K., »ich dachte, ich wäre verhaftet.« K. fragte mit einem gewissen Trotz, denn obwohl sein Handschlag nicht angenommen worden war, fühlte er sich, insbesondere seitdem der Aufseher aufgestanden war, immer unabhängiger von allen diesen Leuten. Er spielte mit ihnen. Er hatte die Absicht, falls sie weggehen sollten, bis zum Haustor nachzulaufen und ihnen seine Verhaftung anzubieten. Darum wiederholte er auch: »Wie kann ich denn in die Bank gehen, da ich verhaftet bin?« »Ach so«, sagte der Aufseher, der schon bei der Tür war, »Sie haben mich mißverstanden. Sie sind verhaftet, gewiß, aber das soll Sie nicht hindern, Ihren Beruf zu erfüllen. Sie sollen auch Ihrer gewöhnlichen Lebensweise nicht gehindert sein.« »Dann ist das Verhaftetsein nicht sehr schlimm«, sagte K. und ging nahe an den Aufseher heran. »Ich meinte es niemals anders«, sagte dieser. »Es scheint aber dann nicht einmal die Mitteilung der Verhaftung sehr notwendig gewesen zu sein«, sagte K. und ging noch näher. Auch die anderen hatten sich genähert. Alle waren jetzt auf einem engen Raum bei der Tür versammelt. »Es war meine Pflicht«, sagte der Aufseher. »Eine dumme Pflicht«, sagte K. unnachgiebig. »Mag sein«, antwortete der Aufseher, »aber wir wollen mit solchen Reden nicht unsere Zeit verlieren. Ich hatte angenommen, daß Sie in die Bank gehen wollen. Da Sie auf alle Worte aufpassen, füge ich hinzu: ich zwinge Sie nicht, in die Bank zu gehen, ich hatte nur angenommen, daß Sie es wollen. Und um Ihnen das zu erleichtern und Ihre Ankunft in der Bank möglichst unauffällig zu machen, habe ich diese drei Herren, Ihre Kollegen, hier zu Ihrer Verfügung gehalten.« »Wie?« rief K. und staunte die drei an. Diese so uncharakteristischen, blutarmen, jungen Leute, die er immer noch nur als Gruppe bei den Photographien in der Erinnerung hatte, waren tatsächlich Beamte aus seiner Bank, nicht Kollegen, das war zu viel gesagt und bewies eine Lücke in der Allwissenheit des Aufsehers, aber untergeordnete Beamte aus der Bank waren es allerdings. Wie hatte K. das übersehen können? Wie hatte er doch hingenommen sein müssen von dem Aufseher und den Wächtern, um diese drei nicht zu erkennen! Den steifen, die Hände schwingenden Rabensteiner, den blonden Kullich mit den tiefliegenden Augen und Kaminer mit dem unausstehlichen, durch eine chronische Muskelzerrung bewirkten Lächeln. »Guten Morgen!« sagte K. nach einem Weilchen und reichte den sich korrekt verbeugenden Herren die Hand. »Ich habe Sie gar nicht erkannt. Nun werden wir also an die Arbeit gehen, nicht?« Die Herren nickten lachend und eifrig, als hätten sie die ganze Zeit über darauf gewartet, nur als K. seinen Hut vermißte, der in seinem Zimmer liegengeblieben war, liefen sie sämtlich hintereinander, ihn holen, was immerhin auf eine gewisse Verlegenheit schließen ließ. K. stand still und sah ihnen durch die zwei offenen Türen nach, der letzte war natürlich der gleichgültige Rabensteiner, der bloß einen eleganten Trab angeschlagen hatte. Kaminer überreichte den Hut, und K. mußte sich, wie dies übrigens auch öfters in der Bank nötig war, ausdrücklich sagen, daß Kaminers Lächeln nicht Absicht war, ja daß er überhaupt absichtlich nicht lächeln konnte. Im Vorzimmer öffnete dann Frau Grubach, die gar nicht sehr schuldbewußt aussah, der ganzen Gesellschaft die Wohnungstür, und K. sah, wie so oft, auf ihr Schürzenband nieder, das so unnötig tief in ihren mächtigen Leib einschnitt. Unten entschloß sich K., die Uhr in der Hand, ein Automobil zu nehmen, um die schon halbstündige Verspätung nicht unnötig zu vergrößern. Kaminer lief zur Ecke, um den Wagen zu holen, die zwei anderen versuchten offensichtlich, K. zu zerstreuen, als plötzlich Kullich auf das gegenüberliegende Haustor zeigte, in dem eben der große Mann mit dem blonden Spitzbart erschien und, im ersten Augenblick ein wenig verlegen darüber, daß er sich jetzt in seiner ganzen Größe zeigte, zur Wand zurücktrat und sich anlehnte. Die Alten waren wohl noch auf der Treppe. K. ärgerte sich über Kullich, daß dieser auf den Mann aufmerksam machte, den er selbst schon früher gesehen, ja den er sogar erwartet hatte. »Schauen Sie nicht hin!« stieß er hervor, ohne zu bemerken, wie auffallend eine solche Redeweise gegenüber selbständigen Männern war. Es war aber auch keine Erklärung nötig, denn gerade kam das Automobil, man setzte sich und fuhr los. Da erinnerte sich K., daß er das Weggehen des Aufsehers und der Wächter gar nicht bemerkt hatte, der Aufseher hatte ihm die drei Beamten verdeckt und nun wieder die Beamten den Aufseher. Viel Geistesgegenwart bewies das nicht, und K. nahm sich vor, sich in dieser Hinsicht genauer zu beobachten. Doch drehte er sich noch unwillkürlich um und beugte sich über das Hinterdeck des Automobils vor, um möglicherweise den Aufseher und die Wächter noch zu sehen. Aber gleich wendete er sich wieder zurück und lehnte sich bequem in die Wagenecke, ohne auch nur den Versuch gemacht zu haben, jemanden zu suchen. Obwohl es nicht den Anschein hatte, hätte er gerade jetzt Zuspruch nötig gehabt, aber nun schienen die Herren ermüdet, Rabensteiner sah rechts aus dem Wagen, Kullich links, und nur Kaminer stand mit seinem Grinsen zur Verfügung, über das einen Spaß zu machen leider die Menschlichkeit verbot.

The gentlemen attacked me first, and now they sit or stand around here and let me ride the High School in front of you. What's the point of phoning a prosecutor if I'm supposedly under arrest? Okay, I won't use the phone.' 'Yes,' said the warden and stretched out his hand to the antechamber where the phone was, 'please make the phone.' human_translations.translator_1: K. stared at the inspector. Was he to be lectured like a schoolboy by what might well be a younger man? To be reprimanded for his openness? And to learn nothing about why he had been arrested and on whose orders? He grew increasingly agitated, paced up and down, freely and without hindrance, pushed his cuffs back, felt his chest, brushed his hair into place, went past the three men, muttering, “It’s completely senseless,” at which they turned and looked at him in a friendly but serious way, and finally came to a stop before the inspector’s table. “Hasterer, the public prosecutor, is a good friend of mine,” he said, “can I telephone him?” “Certainly,” said the inspector, “but I don’t see what sense it makes, unless you have some private matter to discuss with him.” “What sense?” K. cried out, more startled than annoyed. “Who do you think you are? You ask what sense it makes, while you stage the most senseless performance imaginable? Wouldn’t it break a heart of stone? First these gentlemen assault me, and now they sit around or stand about and put me through my paces before you. What sense is there in telephoning a lawyer when I’ve supposedly been arrested? Fine, I won’t telephone.” “But do,” said the inspector, and waved toward the hall, where the telephone was, “please do telephone.” “No, I no longer wish to,” K. said, and went to the window. Across the way the group was still at the window, their peaceful observation now slightly disturbed as K. stepped to the window. The three immediately retreated a few steps, the old couple even withdrawing behind the man, who shielded them with his broad body and, judging by the movement of his lips, apparently said something that couldn’t be understood at that distance. They didn’t disappear entirely, however, but instead seemed to wait for the moment when they could approach the window again unnoticed. “Obnoxious, thoughtless people!” said K., turning back to the room. The inspector may have agreed with him, as he thought he noticed with a sideways glance. But it was equally possible he hadn’t been listening at all, for he had pressed his hand firmly down on the table and seemed to be comparing the length of his fingers. The two guards were sitting on a chest draped with an embroidered coverlet, rubbing their knees. The three young men had placed their hands on their hips and were gazing around aimlessly. Everything was silent, as in some deserted office. “Now, gentlemen,” K. said firmly, and for a moment it seemed to him as if he bore them all upon his shoulders, “judging by your expressions, this affair of mine must be closed. In my view, it would be best to stop worrying whether or not your actions were justified and end the matter on a note of reconciliation, by shaking hands. If you share my view, then please—” and he stepped up to the inspector’s table and held out his hand. The inspector looked up, chewed his lip, and regarded K.’s outstretched hand; K. still believed that the inspector would grasp it. But instead he rose, lifted a hard bowler from Fräulein Bürstner’s bed, and donned it carefully with both hands, like someone trying on a new hat. “How simple everything seems to you!” he said to K. as he did so. “So you think we should end this matter on a note of reconciliation? No, I’m afraid we really can’t. Although that’s not at all to say you should despair. Why should you? You’re under arrest, that’s all. I was to inform you of that, I’ve done so, and I’ve noted your reaction. That’s enough for today, and we can take our leave, temporarily of course. He was toying with them. If they did leave, he intended to follow them to the door of the building and offer to let them arrest him. And so he said again: “How can I go to the bank if I’m under arrest?” “Oh, I see,” said the inspector, who was already at the door, “you’ve misunderstood me; you’re under arrest, certainly, but that’s not meant to keep you from carrying on your profession. The others had approached as well. Everyone was now gathered in a small area by the door. “It was my duty,” said the inspector. “A stupid duty,” said K. relentlessly. “Perhaps so,” replied the inspector, “but let’s not waste our time with such talk. "What sense would there be in that ?" cried K., more in amazement than exasperation. "What kind of man are you, then? You ask me to be sensible and you carry on in the most senseless way imaginable yourself! It's enough to sicken the dogs. People first fall upon me in my own house and then lounge about the room and put me through my paces for your benefit. What sense would there be in telephoning to a lawyer when I'm supposed to be under arrest? All right, I won't telephone." "But do telephone if you want to," replied the Inspector, waving an arm toward the entrance hail, where the telephone was, "please do telephone." "No, I don't want to now," said K., going over to the window. K. stood where he was and watched them through the open double doorway, the last to go, of course, was the apathetic Rabensteiner who had broken into no more than an elegant trot. Kaminer got to the hat and K., as he often had to do at the bank, forcibly reminded himself that the grin was not deliberate, that he in fact wasn't able to grin deliberately. At that moment Mrs. Grubach opened the door from the hallway into the living room where all the people were. She did not seem to feel guilty about anything at all, and K., as often before, looked down at the belt of her apron which, for no reason, cut so deeply into her hefty body. Once downstairs, K., with his watch in his hand, decided to take a taxi - he had already been delayed by half an hour and there was no need to make the delay any longer. Kaminer ran to the corner to summon it, and the two others were making obvious efforts to keep K. diverted when Kullich pointed to the doorway of the house on the other side of the street where the large man with the blonde goatee beard appeared and, a little embarrassed at first at letting himself be seen in his full height, stepped back to the wall and leant against it. The old couple were probably still on the stairs. K. was cross with Kullich for pointing out this man whom he had already seen himself, in fact whom he had been expecting. " Don't look at him!" he snapped, without noticing how odd it was to speak to free men in this way. But there was no explanation needed anyway as just then the taxi arrived, they sat inside and set off. Inside the taxi, K. remembered that he had not noticed the supervisor and the policemen leaving - the supervisor had stopped him noticing the three bank staff and now the three bank staff had stopped him noticing the supervisor. This showed that K. was not very attentive, and he resolved to watch himself more carefully in this respect. Nonetheless, he gave it no thought as he twisted himself round and leant over onto the rear shelf of the car to catch sight of the supervisor and the policemen if he could. But he turned back round straight away and leant comfortably into the corner of the taxi without even having made the effort to see anyone. Although it did not seem like it, now was just the time when he needed some encouragement, but the gentlemen seemed tired just then, Rabensteiner looked out of the car to the right, Kullich to the left and only Kaminer was there with his grin at K.'s service. It would have been inhumane to make fun of that.

translation: K. stared at the warden. Could he possibly be getting lessons in obedience from someone younger than himself? Was he being punished for his openness? And was he to learn nothing about the reason for his arrest or who had ordered it? He became agitated, paced back and forth, unhindered by anyone, pushed back his cuffs, felt his chest, smoothed his hair, passed the three gentlemen and said, "It's pointless," whereupon they turned to face him, approaching him with a courteous but serious demeanor, and finally came to a halt before the warden's desk again. "Prosecutor Hasterer is a good friend of mine," he said, "can I make a telephone call?" "Certainly," said the warden, "but I don't see what sense that would serve, unless it's that you have some private matter to discuss with him." "What sense?" exclaimed K., more startled than annoyed. "Who are you? You talk about sense and carry out the most pointless thing imaginable! Is it not beyond belief? The gentlemen attacked me first, and now they are sitting or standing here and letting me lecture you. What sense would there be in telephoning a prosecutor if I was supposedly arrested? Well, I won't call." "But do," said the warden, stretching his hand toward the anteroom where the telephone was, "please, do make the call." "No, I won't," said K. and went to the window. Across the way, the other people were still gathered at the window and seemed only now, by K.'s approaching, to be slightly disturbed in their quiet observation. The older men wanted to rise, but the man behind them calmed them. "Look, there are also spectators," K. shouted loudly to the warden, pointing with his finger outward. "Away from there!" he then called across. The three immediately stepped back a few paces, the two old men even behind the man who covered them with his broad body, and, judging by his mouth movements, was saying something unintelligible in the distance. They did not completely disappear, though, but seemed to be waiting for the moment when they could approach the window again unnoticed. "Intruding, inconsiderate people!" said K., as he turned back to the room. The warden possibly agreed, as K. believed, with a sidelong glance, but it was equally possible that he hadn't even been listening, for he had a hand firmly pressed on the table and seemed to be comparing the length of his fingers. The two guards were sitting on a trunk covered with a decorative cloth and rubbing their knees. The three young men had their hands on their hips and looked around aimlessly. It was as silent as in some forgotten office. "Well, gentlemen," K. said, it seemed to him for a moment as if he carried them all on his shoulders, "Judging by your appearance, my affair must be finished. I believe it's best not to dwell on the justification or lack thereof of your actions and to give the matter a conciliatory conclusion with a handshake. If you also agree with this, then please—" and he walked towards the warden's desk and extended his hand. The warden raised his eyes, gnawed on his lips and looked at K.'s outstretched hand; K. still believed the warden would strike. However, the warden stood up, took a hard, round hat that lay on Miss Bürstner's bed, and carefully placed it on his head with both hands, as one does when trying on a new hat. "How simple everything seems to you!" he said to K. "We should give the matter a conciliatory conclusion, did you say? No, no, that's really not possible. Which is not to say, of course, that you should despair. No, why should you? You are simply arrested, that's all. I told you that, I did, and I also saw how you received it. That's enough for today and we can say goodbye, although only provisionally. You'll probably want to go to the bank now?" "To the bank?" asked K., "I thought I was arrested." K. asked with a certain defiance, because although his handshake had not been accepted, he felt, especially since the warden had stood up, increasingly independent of all these people. He was playing with them. He intended, if they should leave, to run after them to the front door and offer them his arrest. Therefore, he repeated: "How can I go to the bank if I am arrested?" "Ah, so," said the warden, already at the door, "you misunderstood me. You are arrested, certainly, but that shouldn't prevent you from fulfilling your duties. Nor should it hinder you from living your usual life." "Then being arrested is not very bad," said K. and moved closer to the warden. "I never meant it any other way," said the warden. "It seems then that even the announcement of the arrest was not very necessary," said K. and moved even closer. All had also moved closer, now all were gathered together in a cramped space by the door. "It was my duty," said the warden. "A stupid duty," said K. stubbornly. "Maybe," replied the warden, "but we don't want to waste our time with such talk. I assumed you wanted to go to the bank. Since you are paying attention to every word, I add: I am not forcing you to go to the bank, I simply assumed you wanted to. And to make it easier for you and to make your arrival at the bank as inconspicuous as possible, I had these three gentlemen, your colleagues, at your disposal." "What?" exclaimed K. and stared at the three. These uncharacteristic, pale, young men, whom he still only remembered as a group in the photographs, were indeed officials from his bank, not colleagues, that was too much to say and proved a gap in the warden's omniscience, but they were subordinate officials from the bank. How could K. have overlooked that? How could he have tolerated being treated by the warden and the guards like this, not to recognize these three! Stiff Rabensteiner, blonde Kullich with his deep-set eyes and Kaminer with his unbearable, chronically muscle-strained smile. "Good morning!" said K. after a while and extended his hand to the three gentlemen, who bowed politely and eagerly as if they had been waiting for this all along. However, just as K. missed his hat, which was still lying in his room, they all ran after it, which did at least suggest some embarrassment. K. stood still and watched them through the two open doors, the last one being the indifferent Rabensteiner, who had simply struck an elegant trot. Kaminer handed over the hat, and K. had to say expressly, as was also often necessary in the bank, that Kaminer's smile was not intentional, that he couldn't actually smile on purpose. In the anteroom, Mrs. Grubach, who did not look very guilty at all, opened the apartment door to the whole company, and K. saw, as often, her apron ribbon tied uncomfortably low on her massive body. Downstairs, K. decided, with the clock in hand, to take a car to avoid unnecessarily increasing the already half-hour delay. Kaminer ran to the corner to fetch the car, the other two obviously tried to distract K., when suddenly Kullich pointed to the opposite doorway, through which the tall man with the blonde mustache appeared, and, initially a little embarrassed about being seen in his full height, stepped back against the wall and leaned against it. The old men were probably still on the stairs. K. got annoyed with Kullich for drawing attention to the man whom he himself had already seen, indeed expected. "Don't look!" he blurted out, without noticing how unusual such a remark was towards independent men. But an explanation was not needed, because just then the car arrived, they got in, and drove off. At that moment, K. remembered that he hadn't even noticed the warden and the guards leaving, the warden had concealed the three officials from him and now the officials the warden. That didn't display much mental acuity, and K. decided to observe himself more closely in this respect. But he involuntarily turned around and leaned over the back of the car, trying to get a glimpse of the warden and the guards. But he immediately turned back and leaned comfortably into the corner of the car, without even trying to look for anyone. Although it didn't seem like it, he would have needed support right now, but now the gentlemen seemed tired, Rabensteiner looked out the right side of the car, Kullich out the left, and only Kaminer stood at attention with his grin, which unfortunately it was humanly impossible to make fun of.
source_text: K. starrte den Aufseher an. Schulmäßige Lehren bekam er hier von einem vielleicht jüngeren Menschen? Für seine Offenheit wurde er mit einer Rüge bestraft? Und über den Grund seiner Verhaftung und über deren Auftraggeber erfuhr er nichts? Er geriet in eine gewisse Aufregung, ging auf und ab, woran ihn niemand hinderte, schob seine Manschetten zurück, befühlte die Brust, strich sein Haar zurecht, kam an den drei Herren vorüber, sagte: »Es ist ja sinnlos«, worauf sich diese zu ihm umdrehten und ihn entgegenkommend, aber ernst ansahen und machte endlich wieder vor dem Tisch des Aufsehers halt. »Der Staatsanwalt Hasterer ist mein guter Freund«, sagte er, »kann ich ihm telephonieren?« »Gewiß«, sagte der Aufseher, »aber ich weiß nicht, welchen Sinn das haben sollte, es müßte denn sein, daß Sie irgendeine private Angelegenheit mit ihm zu besprechen haben.« »Welchen Sinn?« rief K., mehr bestürzt als geärgert. »Wer sind Sie denn? Sie wollen einen Sinn und führen das Sinnloseste auf, das es gibt? Ist es nicht zum Steinerweichen? Die Herren haben mich zuerst überfallen, und jetzt sitzen oder stehen sie hier herum und lassen mich vor Ihnen die Hohe Schule reiten. Welchen Sinn es hätte, an einen Staatsanwalt zu telephonieren, wenn ich angeblich verhaftet bin? Gut, ich werde nicht telephonieren.« »Aber doch«, sagte der Aufseher und streckte die Hand zum Vorzimmer aus, wo das Telephon war, »bitte, telephonieren Sie doch.« »Nein, ich will nicht mehr«, sagte K. und ging zum Fenster. Drüben war noch die Gesellschaft beim Fenster und schien nur jetzt dadurch, daß K. ans Fenster herangetreten war, in der Ruhe des Zuschauens ein wenig gestört. Die Alten wollten sich erheben, aber der Mann hinter ihnen beruhigte sie. »Dort sind auch solche Zuschauer«, rief K. ganz laut dem Aufseher zu und zeigte mit dem Zeigefinger hinaus. »Weg von dort«, rief er dann hinüber. Die drei wichen auch sofort ein paar Schritte zurück, die beiden Alten sogar noch hinter den Mann, der sie mit seinem breiten Körper deckte und, nach seinen Mundbewegungen zu schließen, irgend etwas auf die Entfernung hin Unverständliches sagte. Ganz aber verschwanden sie nicht, sondern schienen auf den Augenblick zu warten, in dem sie sich unbemerkt wieder dem Fenster nähern könnten. »Zudringliche, rücksichtslose Leute!« sagte K., als er sich ins Zimmer zurückwendete. Der Aufseher stimmte ihm möglicherweise zu, wie K. mit einem Seitenblick zu erkennen glaubte. Aber es war ebensogut möglich, daß er gar nicht zugehört hatte, denn er hatte eine Hand fest auf den Tisch gedrückt und schien die Finger ihrer Länge nach zu vergleichen. Die zwei Wächter saßen auf einem mit einer Schmuckdecke verhüllten Koffer und rieben ihre Knie. Die drei jungen Leute hatten die Hände in die Hüften gelegt und sahen ziellos herum. Es war still wie in irgendeinem vergessenen Büro. »Nun, meine Herren«, rief K., es schien ihm einen Augenblick lang, als trage er alle auf seinen Schultern, »Ihrem Aussehen nach zu schließen, dürfte meine Angelegenheit beendet sein. Ich bin der Ansicht, daß es am besten ist, über die Berechtigung oder Nichtberechtigung Ihres Vorgehens nicht mehr nachzudenken und der Sache durch einen gegenseitigen Händedruck einen versöhnlichen Abschluß zu geben. Wenn auch Sie meiner Ansicht sind, dann bitte –« und er trat an den Tisch des Aufsehers hin und reichte ihm die Hand. Der Aufseher hob die Augen, nagte an den Lippen und sah auf K.s ausgestreckte Hand; noch immer glaubte K., der Aufseher werde einschlagen. Dieser aber stand auf, nahm einen harten, runden Hut, der auf Fräulein Bürstners Bett lag, und setzte sich ihn vorsichtig mit beiden Händen auf, wie man es bei der Anprobe neuer Hüte tut. »Wie einfach Ihnen alles scheint!« sagte er dabei zu K. »wir sollten der Sache einen versöhnlichen Abschluß geben, meinten Sie? Nein, nein, das geht wirklich nicht. Womit ich andererseits durchaus nicht sagen will, daß Sie verzweifeln sollen. Nein, warum denn? Sie sind nur verhaftet, nichts weiter. Das hatte ich Ihnen mitzuteilen, habe es getan und habe auch gesehen, wie Sie es aufgenommen haben. Damit ist es für heute genug und wir können uns verabschieden, allerdings nur vorläufig. Sie werden wohl jetzt in die Bank gehen wollen?« »In die Bank?« fragte K., »ich dachte, ich wäre verhaftet.« K. fragte mit einem gewissen Trotz, denn obwohl sein Handschlag nicht angenommen worden war, fühlte er sich, insbesondere seitdem der Aufseher aufgestanden war, immer unabhängiger von allen diesen Leuten. Er spielte mit ihnen. Er hatte die Absicht, falls sie weggehen sollten, bis zum Haustor nachzulaufen und ihnen seine Verhaftung anzubieten. Darum wiederholte er auch: »Wie kann ich denn in die Bank gehen, da ich verhaftet bin?« »Ach so«, sagte der Aufseher, der schon bei der Tür war, »Sie haben mich mißverstanden. Sie sind verhaftet, gewiß, aber das soll Sie nicht hindern, Ihren Beruf zu erfüllen. Sie sollen auch Ihrer gewöhnlichen Lebensweise nicht gehindert sein.« »Dann ist das Verhaftetsein nicht sehr schlimm«, sagte K. und ging nahe an den Aufseher heran. »Ich meinte es niemals anders«, sagte dieser. »Es scheint aber dann nicht einmal die Mitteilung der Verhaftung sehr notwendig gewesen zu sein«, sagte K. und ging noch näher. Auch die anderen hatten sich genähert. Alle waren jetzt auf einem engen Raum bei der Tür versammelt. »Es war meine Pflicht«, sagte der Aufseher. »Eine dumme Pflicht«, sagte K. unnachgiebig. »Mag sein«, antwortete der Aufseher, »aber wir wollen mit solchen Reden nicht unsere Zeit verlieren. Ich hatte angenommen, daß Sie in die Bank gehen wollen. Da Sie auf alle Worte aufpassen, füge ich hinzu: ich zwinge Sie nicht, in die Bank zu gehen, ich hatte nur angenommen, daß Sie es wollen. Und um Ihnen das zu erleichtern und Ihre Ankunft in der Bank möglichst unauffällig zu machen, habe ich diese drei Herren, Ihre Kollegen, hier zu Ihrer Verfügung gehalten.« »Wie?« rief K. und staunte die drei an. Diese so uncharakteristischen, blutarmen, jungen Leute, die er immer noch nur als Gruppe bei den Photographien in der Erinnerung hatte, waren tatsächlich Beamte aus seiner Bank, nicht Kollegen, das war zu viel gesagt und bewies eine Lücke in der Allwissenheit des Aufsehers, aber untergeordnete Beamte aus der Bank waren es allerdings. Wie hatte K. das übersehen können? Wie hatte er doch hingenommen sein müssen von dem Aufseher und den Wächtern, um diese drei nicht zu erkennen! Den steifen, die Hände schwingenden Rabensteiner, den blonden Kullich mit den tiefliegenden Augen und Kaminer mit dem unausstehlichen, durch eine chronische Muskelzerrung bewirkten Lächeln. »Guten Morgen!« sagte K. nach einem Weilchen und reichte den sich korrekt verbeugenden Herren die Hand. »Ich habe Sie gar nicht erkannt. Nun werden wir also an die Arbeit gehen, nicht?« Die Herren nickten lachend und eifrig, als hätten sie die ganze Zeit über darauf gewartet, nur als K. seinen Hut vermißte, der in seinem Zimmer liegengeblieben war, liefen sie sämtlich hintereinander, ihn holen, was immerhin auf eine gewisse Verlegenheit schließen ließ. K. stand still und sah ihnen durch die zwei offenen Türen nach, der letzte war natürlich der gleichgültige Rabensteiner, der bloß einen eleganten Trab angeschlagen hatte. Kaminer überreichte den Hut, und K. mußte sich, wie dies übrigens auch öfters in der Bank nötig war, ausdrücklich sagen, daß Kaminers Lächeln nicht Absicht war, ja daß er überhaupt absichtlich nicht lächeln konnte. Im Vorzimmer öffnete dann Frau Grubach, die gar nicht sehr schuldbewußt aussah, der ganzen Gesellschaft die Wohnungstür, und K. sah, wie so oft, auf ihr Schürzenband nieder, das so unnötig tief in ihren mächtigen Leib einschnitt. Unten entschloß sich K., die Uhr in der Hand, ein Automobil zu nehmen, um die schon halbstündige Verspätung nicht unnötig zu vergrößern. Kaminer lief zur Ecke, um den Wagen zu holen, die zwei anderen versuchten offensichtlich, K. zu zerstreuen, als plötzlich Kullich auf das gegenüberliegende Haustor zeigte, in dem eben der große Mann mit dem blonden Spitzbart erschien und, im ersten Augenblick ein wenig verlegen darüber, daß er sich jetzt in seiner ganzen Größe zeigte, zur Wand zurücktrat und sich anlehnte. Die Alten waren wohl noch auf der Treppe. K. ärgerte sich über Kullich, daß dieser auf den Mann aufmerksam machte, den er selbst schon früher gesehen, ja den er sogar erwartet hatte. »Schauen Sie nicht hin!« stieß er hervor, ohne zu bemerken, wie auffallend eine solche Redeweise gegenüber selbständigen Männern war. Es war aber auch keine Erklärung nötig, denn gerade kam das Automobil, man setzte sich und fuhr los. Da erinnerte sich K., daß er das Weggehen des Aufsehers und der Wächter gar nicht bemerkt hatte, der Aufseher hatte ihm die drei Beamten verdeckt und nun wieder die Beamten den Aufseher. Viel Geistesgegenwart bewies das nicht, und K. nahm sich vor, sich in dieser Hinsicht genauer zu beobachten. Doch drehte er sich noch unwillkürlich um und beugte sich über das Hinterdeck des Automobils vor, um möglicherweise den Aufseher und die Wächter noch zu sehen. Aber gleich wendete er sich wieder zurück und lehnte sich bequem in die Wagenecke, ohne auch nur den Versuch gemacht zu haben, jemanden zu suchen. Obwohl es nicht den Anschein hatte, hätte er gerade jetzt Zuspruch nötig gehabt, aber nun schienen die Herren ermüdet, Rabensteiner sah rechts aus dem Wagen, Kullich links, und nur Kaminer stand mit seinem Grinsen zur Verfügung, über das einen Spaß zu machen leider die Menschlichkeit verbot.

human_translations.translator_1: K. stared at the inspector. Was he to be lectured like a schoolboy by what might well be a younger man? To be reprimanded for his openness? And to learn nothing about why he had been arrested and on whose orders? He grew increasingly agitated, paced up and down, freely and without hindrance, pushed his cuffs back, felt his chest, brushed his hair into place, went past the three men, muttering, “It’s completely senseless,” at which they turned and looked at him in a friendly but serious way, and finally came to a stop before the inspector’s table. “Hasterer, the public prosecutor, is a good friend of mine,” he said, “can I telephone him?” “Certainly,” said the inspector, “but I don’t see what sense it makes, unless you have some private matter to discuss with him.” “What sense?” K. cried out, more startled than annoyed. “Who do you think you are? You ask what sense it makes, while you stage the most senseless performance imaginable? Wouldn’t it break a heart of stone? First these gentlemen assault me, and now they sit around or stand about and put me through my paces before you. What sense is there in telephoning a lawyer when I’ve supposedly been arrested? Fine, I won’t telephone.” “But do,” said the inspector, and waved toward the hall, where the telephone was, “please do telephone.” “No, I no longer wish to,” K. said, and went to the window. Across the way the group was still at the window, their peaceful observation now slightly disturbed as K. stepped to the window. The old couple started to rise, but the man behind them calmed them down. “There’s more of the audience over there,” K. cried out to the inspector and pointed outside. “Get away from there,” he yelled at them. The three immediately retreated a few steps, the old couple even withdrawing behind the man, who shielded them with his broad body and, judging by the movement of his lips, apparently said something that couldn’t be understood at that distance. They didn’t disappear entirely, however, but instead seemed to wait for the moment when they could approach the window again unnoticed. “Obnoxious, thoughtless people!” said K., turning back to the room. The inspector may have agreed with him, as he thought he noticed with a sideways glance. But it was equally possible he hadn’t been listening at all, for he had pressed his hand firmly down on the table and seemed to be comparing the length of his fingers. The two guards were sitting on a chest draped with an embroidered coverlet, rubbing their knees. The three young men had placed their hands on their hips and were gazing around aimlessly. Everything was silent, as in some deserted office. “Now, gentlemen,” K. said firmly, and for a moment it seemed to him as if he bore them all upon his shoulders, “judging by your expressions, this affair of mine must be closed. In my view, it would be best to stop worrying whether or not your actions were justified and end the matter on a note of reconciliation, by shaking hands. If you share my view, then please—” and he stepped up to the inspector’s table and held out his hand. The inspector looked up, chewed his lip, and regarded K.’s outstretched hand; K. still believed that the inspector would grasp it. But instead he rose, lifted a hard bowler from Fräulein Bürstner’s bed, and donned it carefully with both hands, like someone trying on a new hat. “How simple everything seems to you!” he said to K. as he did so. “So you think we should end this matter on a note of reconciliation? No, I’m afraid we really can’t. Although that’s not at all to say you should despair. Why should you? You’re under arrest, that’s all. I was to inform you of that, I’ve done so, and I’ve noted your reaction. That’s enough for today, and we can take our leave, temporarily of course. No doubt you wish to go to the bank now?” “To the bank?” K. asked. “I thought I was under arrest.” K. said this with a certain insistence, for although no one had shaken his hand, he was beginning to feel increasingly independent of these people, particularly once the inspector had stood up. He was toying with them. If they did leave, he intended to follow them to the door of the building and offer to let them arrest him. And so he said again: “How can I go to the bank if I’m under arrest?” “Oh, I see,” said the inspector, who was already at the door, “you’ve misunderstood me; you’re under arrest, certainly, but that’s not meant to keep you from carrying on your profession. Nor are you to be hindered in the course of your ordinary life.” “Then being under arrest isn’t so bad,” said K., approaching the inspector. “I never said it was,” he replied. “But in that case even the notification of arrest scarcely seems necessary,” said K., stepping closer still. The others had approached as well. Everyone was now gathered in a small area by the door. “It was my duty,” said the inspector. “A stupid duty,” said K. relentlessly. “Perhaps so,” replied the inspector, “but let’s not waste our time with such talk. I assumed you wished to go to the bank. Since you weigh every word so carefully, let me add that I’m not forcing you to go to the bank , I simply assumed you would want to. And to facilitate that, and to render your arrival at the bank as inconspicuous as possible, I’ve arranged for three of your colleagues here to be placed at your disposal.” “What?” K. cried out, and stared at the three in amazement. These so uncharacteristically anemic young men, whom he recalled only as a group by the photographs, were indeed clerks from his bank, not colleagues, that would be an overstatement, and indicated a gap in the inspector’s omniscience, but they were certainly lower-level clerks from the bank. How could K. have failed to notice that? How preoccupied he must have been by the inspector and the guards not to recognize these three. Wooden, arm-swinging Rabensteiner, blond Kullich with his deep-set eyes, and Kaminer with his annoying smile, produced by a chronic muscular twitch. “Good morning!” K. said after a moment, and held out his hand to the men, who bowed courteously. “I completely failed to recognize you. So now we can go to work, right?” The men nodded, laughing and eager, as if that was what they’d been waiting for all along, but when K. missed his hat, which he’d left in his room, all three tripped over each other’s heels to get it, which indicated a certain embarrassment on their part after all. K. stood still and watched them pass through the two open doors, the lethargic Rabensteiner bringing up the rear, of course, having broken into no more than an elegant trot. Kaminer handed over the hat and K. had to remind himself, as he often did at the bank, that Kaminer’s smile was not deliberate and that in fact he couldn’t smile deliberately at all. In the hall, Frau Grubach, not looking as if she felt any particular sense of guilt, opened the outer door for the whole company and K. looked down, as so often, at her apron strings, which cut so unnecessarily deeply into her robust body. Downstairs, watch in hand, K. decided to go by car so as not to extend unnecessarily what was already a half-hour delay. Kaminer ran to the corner to get a cab; the other two apparently felt they should entertain K. somehow, since Kullich suddenly pointed to the door of the building across the way, in which the man with the blond goatee had just appeared, and, at first embarrassed by now showing himself full-length, had retreated to the wall and leaned against it. The old couple were probably still on the stairs. K. was annoyed at Kullich for having pointed out the man, since he had already seen him himself, and in fact had been expecting him. “Don’t look over there,” he said quickly, without realizing how strange it must sound to speak that way to grown men. But no explanation was necessary, for at that moment the cab arrived, they got in, and it pulled away. Then K. remembered that he hadn’t seen the inspector and the guards leave: the inspector had diverted his attention from the three clerks, and now the clerks had done the same for the inspector. That didn’t show much presence of mind, and K. resolved to pay greater attention to such things. Even now he turned around involuntarily and leaned across the rear panel of the car to see if the inspector and guards might still be in sight. But he turned around again immediately, without having made the slightest effort to locate anyone, and leaned back comfortably into the corner of the cab. Despite appearances, he could have used some conversation, but now the men seemed tired : Rabensteiner gazed out of the car to the right, and Kullych to the left, leaving only Kaminer and his grin, which common decency unfortunately forbade as a topic of humor.
