Why do you speak of a hundred years?” The generals said, “One day in heaven is equal to one year on earth.” The Great Sage said, “I am glad to tell you that the Jade Emperor was kind to me this time, and gave me the title of being Equal to Heaven, and let me live in the Palace of the Equal of Heaven, and I had servants to wait on me. Seeing that I had nothing to do, he appointed me to look after the Peach Orchard. Then followed the great Banquet of the Queen of Heaven. Because I was not invited to it, I went to the Celestial Lake Palace where the banquet was to be held, and finding none of the guests had arrived and that everything had been prepared and all the dishes laid out, I stealthily tasted them and drank the wine. On leaving I lost my way and got into the Mansion of the Ancient of Days, where I found five gourds full of the Pills of Immortality. These I also stealthily swallowed. Fearing that the Jade Emperor might find fault with me, I left Heaven altogether and returned here.”
human_translations.translator_3: The elixir immediately woke him from his intoxication and enabled him to make a sober analysis of the situation. “Bad! Very bad! Down to earth, where I’ll go back to being a king.” In the interest of discretion, he chose the West Gate rather than the South Gate out of Heaven (having taken the precaution of making himself invisible first) and landed on Flower-Fruit Mountain. “I’m back, little ones!” he announced. The throng of monkeys and cave demons—then in the middle of their military training—dropped their weapons in surprise and kneeled. “You were enjoying yourself so much in Heaven, you forgot all about us,” they said reproachfully. “But I’ve only been gone half a year!” Monkey laughed, sweeping back onto his throne. “Remember that one day in Heaven is a year on earth,” his generals reminded him. “You’ve been gone well over a century. What job did the Jade Emperor give you this time?” “This time,” Monkey reported, “the Jade Emperor saw sense and appointed me Great Sage Equal to Heaven. He built me a palace and gave me two departments and a ministerial staff. But it turned out that I had nothing to do, so they put me in charge of the Orchard of Immortal Peaches. When the Queen Mother failed to invite me to a banquet, I crashed her palace and secretly guzzled all the food and wine for the feast. Then I stumbled by mistake into Laozi’s palace, and since he wasn’t around I polished off all his elixirs. After that, I decided to lie low for a while. So here I am.”
human_translations.translator_4: Before long he was full of pills and quite sober. “This is terrible,” he thought, “this is a colossal disaster. If the Jade Emperor is shocked by this, I'm done for. I must get out of here. I'd be much better off as a king in the lower world.” He rushed out of the Tushita Palace, avoiding his usual route. Using a spell to make himself invisible, he left by the West Gate of Heaven, and went straight down to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit by cloud. When he got there he saw flags, banners, spears and halberds gleaming in the sun: the four Stalwart Generals and the seventy-two kings of the monsters were holding military exercises. “Children, I'm back,” shouted the Great Sage in a loud voice, and all the fiends dropped their weapons and fell to their knees. “You don't care, do you, Great Sage?” they said. “It's been so long since you left us, and you never came back to see us.” “I haven't been long, I haven't been long,” protested the Great Sage, and as they talked they walked into the innermost part of the cave. When the four Stalwart General's had tidied the place up and made him sit down, they kowtowed to him and asked, “What office did you hold, Great Sage, during your century and more in Heaven?” The Great Sage laughed and said, “As far as I can remember it was only six months, so why do you say it was over a century?” “A day in Heaven is the same as a year on earth,” the Stalwart Generals replied. “I was lucky this time,” said the Great Sage. “The Jade Emperor took a liking to me and ennobled me as the Great Sage Equaling Heaven. He had an Equaling Heaven Residence built for me, complete with a Tranquillity Office and a Calm Divinity Office with Immortal functionaries, attendants and guards. Later on, when he saw that I had nothing to do, he put me in charge of the Peach Orchard. Recently the Queen Mother Goddess gave a Peach Banquet, but she didn't invite me. Instead of waiting for an invitation, I went to the Jade Pool and stole all the immortal food and drink. I staggered away from the Jade Pool and blundered into Lord Lao Zi's palace, and there I ate up his five gourds of pills of immortality. Then I got out through the heavenly gates and came here because I was scared that the Jade Emperor was going to punish me.”

translation: Yesterday morning the prince was here; among other things, he persuaded me to move to his dacha. I knew he would insist on this, and I was sure he would blurt out to me that it would be "easier to die among people and trees" on the dacha, as he puts it. But today he didn't say "die," but "it will be easier to live," which, however, is almost the same for me, in my situation. I asked him what he meant by his constant "trees" and why he was imposing them on me so, and I was surprised to learn that I had supposedly said that evening that I was coming to Pavlovsk for the last time to look at the trees. When I pointed out to him that it makes no difference whether you die under the trees or looking out the window at my bricks, and that there's no need to make such a fuss for two weeks, he immediately agreed; but, in his opinion, the greenery and fresh air would certainly produce some physical change in me, and my agitation and my dreams would change and perhaps ease. I again remarked to him, laughing, that he speaks like a materialist. He replied to me with his smile that he had always been a materialist. Since he never lies, these words mean something. His smile is beautiful; I saw him more attentively now. I don't know if I love him or not now; I don't have time for that now. My five-month-long hatred for him, it should be noted, has been waning completely in the last month. Who knows, perhaps I came to Pavlovsk, primarily, to see him. But... why did I leave my room then? A condemned man should not leave his corner; and if I had not made a final decision now, and had decided instead to wait until the last moment, then, of course, I would not have left my room for anything and would not have accepted his offer to "die" with him in Pavlovsk.
source_text: «Вчера утром был у меня князь; между прочим, он уговорил меня переехать на свою дачу. Я так и знал, что он непременно будет на этом настаивать, и уверен был, что он так прямо и брякнет мне, что мне на даче будет «легче умирать между людьми и деревьями», как он выражается. Но сегодня он не сказал умереть, а сказал «будет легче прожить», что, однако же, почти все равно для меня, в моем положении. Я спросил его, что он подразумевает под своими беспрерывными «деревьями» и почему он мне так навязывает эти «деревья», — и с удивлением узнал от него, что я сам будто бы на том вечере выразился, что приезжал в Павловск в последний раз посмотреть на деревья. Когда я заметил ему, что ведь всё равно умирать, что под деревьями, что смотря в окно на мои кирпичи, и что для двух недель нечего так церемониться, то он тотчас же согласился; но зелень и чистый воздух, по его мнению, непременно произведут во мне какую-нибудь физическую перемену, и мое волнение и мои сны переменятся и, может быть, облегчатся. Я опять заметил ему смеясь, что он говорит как материалист. Он ответил мне с своею улыбкой, что он и всегда был материалист. Так как он никогда не лжет, то эти слова что-нибудь да означают. Улыбка его хороша; я разглядел его теперь внимательнее. Я не знаю, люблю или не люблю я его теперь; теперь мне некогда с этим возиться. Моя пятимесячная ненависть к нему, надо заметить, в последний месяц стала совсем утихать. Кто знает, может быть, я приезжал в Павловск, главное, чтоб его увидать. Но... зачем я оставлял тогда мою комнату? Приговоренный к смерти не должен оставлять своего угла; и если бы теперь я не принял окончательного решения, а решился бы, напротив, ждать до последнего часу, то, конечно, не оставил бы моей комнаты ни за что и не принял бы предложения переселиться к нему «умирать» в Павловск.

I asked him what he meant by his uninterrupted "trees" and why he imposed these "trees" on me like that, and I was surprised to learn from him that I myself allegedly said that evening that I had come to Pavlovsk for the last time to see on the trees. I again remarked to him, laughing, that he was talking like a materialist. He answered me with his smile that he had always been a materialist. Since he never lies, these words mean something. His smile is good; I took a closer look at it now. I don't know whether I love him or not now; Now I don't have time to deal with it. My five-month hatred for him, it should be noted, has begun to subside completely in the last month. Who knows, maybe I came to Pavlovsk, the main thing is to see him. But... why did I leave my room then? He who is condemned to death must not leave his corner; and if now I had not made a final decision, but, on the contrary, had decided to wait until the last hour, then, of course, I would not have left my room for anything and would not have accepted the offer to move to him “to die” in Pavlovsk.

Но сегодня он не сказал умереть, а сказал «будет легче прожить», что, однако же, почти все равно для меня, в моем положении. Я спросил его, что он подразумевает под своими беспрерывными «деревьями» и почему он мне так навязывает эти «деревья», — и с удивлением узнал от него, что я сам будто бы на том вечере выразился, что приезжал в Павловск в последний раз посмотреть на деревья. translation: Suddenly, a macaque leapt out from the group, calling out in a loud voice, "Your Majesty, if you are thinking so far ahead, it is truly a display of an enlightened mind! Nowadays, among all living creatures, there are only three who are beyond the control of Yama, the King of Hell." The Monkey King said, "Do you know who these three are?" The macaque replied, "They are the Buddha, the Immortal, and the Divine. They have escaped the cycle of reincarnation and are neither born nor destroyed, living as long as heaven, earth, mountains, and rivers." The Monkey King said, "Where do these three reside?" The macaque answered, "They are only in the world of Jambudvipa, within the ancient caves of Mount Xumi." Hearing this, the Monkey King was filled with joy and said, "Tomorrow, I shall bid you farewell and descend the mountain. I will travel to the ends of the earth, venturing far and wide to seek out these three, and learn the secret of eternal life and immortality, so as to forever evade the clutches of Yama." Ah! That very sentence shattered the net of reincarnation, leading to the becoming of the Great Sage, Equalling Heaven. All the other monkeys clapped their hands in praise, saying, "Well done! Well done! We shall climb the mountain tomorrow to gather fruits and prepare a grand feast to send off our Great King!"

Napoleon shuddered, thought for a moment, and said to me: "You have reminded me of the third heart that loves me; thank you, my friend!" He immediately sat down and wrote that letter to Josephine, which the next day was sent off with Constant.

source_text: Точно вечность уже осеняла его мрачным крылом своим. Иногда, по ночам, мы проводили целые часы одни, молча, — мамелюк Рустан храпит, бывало, в соседней комнате; ужасно крепко спал этот человек. «Зато он верен мне и династии», — говорил про него Наполеон. Однажды мне было страшно больно, и вдруг он заметил слезы на глазах моих; он посмотрел на меня с умилением: «Ты жалеешь меня! — вскричал он, — ты, дитя, да еще, может быть, пожалеет меня и другой ребенок, мой сын, le roi de Rome[27]; остальные все, все меня ненавидят, а братья первые продадут меня в несчастии!». Я зарыдал и бросился к нему; тут и он не выдержал; мы обнялись, и слезы наши смешались. «Напишите, напишите письмо к императрице Жозефине!» — прорыдал я ему. Наполеон вздрогнул, подумал и сказал мне: «Ты напомнил мне о третьем сердце, которое меня любит; благодарю тебя, друг мой!». Тут же сел и написал то письмо к Жозефине, с которым назавтра же был отправлен Констан.

translation:
Thousand officials with jeweled ornaments surround the throne, the five guards' banners stand guard on both sides. Holding gold gourds and axes, they stand in pairs; red silk candles and incense from royal censors fill the hall with a magnificent aroma. Dragons soar and phoenixes dance, falcons and eagles ascend; the holy emperor's presence shines, loyal and righteous ministers gather close. 

Passing over millennia to surpass Shun and Yu, ascending to a thousand generations to rival Yao and Tang. I see the royal scepter and the dragon robes, their brilliance intermingling; jade bracelets and jeweled fans, auspicious clouds gently wafting. Crowns of jewels, belts of jade, purple sashes and gold emblems.  A thousand troops guard the imperial carriage, with two lines of courtiers attending. The emperor bathes, devoutly respecting the Buddha, converting to the good fruit, joyfully taking incense.

King Tang, in his grand procession, arrives early at the temple gates, silencing the music and ceremonial instruments, disembarks from his carriage, and leads his retinue of officials. They bow and take incense before the Buddha. After three circumambulations, he lifts his head to admire the beautiful sacred grounds. Look! The banners flutter and the jeweled canopy shines. Banners flutter and sway, condensing the emptiness, a rainbow cascade of colors; the jeweled canopy shines, reflecting the sun, red sparks flash with brilliance. 

The Buddha’s golden image, majestic, the Arhats' jade faces, awe-inspiring.  Bottles of fragrant flowers stand, sandalwood incense smolders, incense permeates the sky. Fresh fruits are arranged on a vermilion platter, exotic candies piled on colorful trays. Great monks recite scriptures, hoping to liberate wandering souls from suffering.

Emperor Taizong, with his ministers, both civil and military, take incense and bow before the Buddha's golden body, then venerate the Arhats.  I see the eminent Master Xuanzang, master of the great hall, leading the monks and bowing to King Tang. After the ceremony, they disperse to meditate, the master presents the Emperor with a scroll titled "Liberating the Perishing" saying:

"Vast virtue, deep and boundless, Zen stillness, utterly silent. Purity, clear and luminous, flowing through the three realms. Infinite transformations, encompassing yin and yang. True nature, boundless and eternal. Observing these lost souls, compassion is deeply called for.

By imperial mandate, I have assembled these monks, to meditate and teach dharma. To widely open the doors of convenience, to launch a great vessel of compassion, to ferry across the suffering sea of life, to liberate all beings from the illness of the six realms. Guide them back to the true path, where freedom reigns in the vastness of creation.

Neither action nor inaction; all is perfectly pure. Relying on this opportune moment, invite the blessings of the grand, pure jade palaces. Utilize this auspicious assembly, to escape the prison of hell and rebirth.

Ascend to the Pure Land and enjoy boundless freedom, traveling to the West at will.

Poetry:

One eternal incense burner, several scrolls of transcendence.

Infinite wondrous dharma proclaimed, limitless divine grace received.

All grudges and entanglements disappear, all wandering souls are liberated.

May my kingdom be blessed with peace and prosperity for ten thousand years."

Emperor Taizong read with great joy and said to the monks, "May you all maintain your pure intentions and never neglect these sacred rituals. When the work is completed, I will bestow great rewards, ensuring your labors are not in vain." 

The twelve hundred monks bowed in unison, expressing their gratitude.
source_text: 千官环佩分前后，五卫旌旗列两旁。执金瓜，擎斧钺，双双对对；绛纱烛，御炉香，霭霭堂堂。龙飞凤舞，鹗荐鹰扬。圣明天子正，忠义大臣良。介福千年过舜禹，升平万代赛尧汤。又见那曲柄伞，滚龙袍，辉光相射；玉连环，彩凤扇，瑞霭飘扬。珠冠玉带，紫绶金章。护驾军千队，扶舆将两行。这皇帝沐浴虔诚尊敬佛，皈依善果喜拈香。唐王大驾，早到寺前，吩咐住了音乐响器，下了车辇，引着多官。拜佛拈香。三匝已毕，抬头观看，果然好座道场，但见：幢幡飘舞，宝盖飞辉。幢幡飘舞，凝空道道彩霞摇；宝盖飞辉，映日翩翩红电彻。世尊金象貌臻臻，罗汉玉容威烈烈。瓶插仙花，炉焚檀降。瓶插仙花，锦树辉辉漫宝刹；炉焚檀降，香云霭霭透清霄。时新果品砌朱盘，奇样糖酥堆彩案。高僧罗列诵真经，愿拔孤魂离苦难。太宗文武俱各拈香，拜了佛祖金身，参了罗汉。又见那大阐都纲陈玄奘法师引众僧罗拜唐王。礼毕，分班各安禅位，法师献上济孤榜文与太宗看，榜曰：“至德渺茫，禅宗寂灭。清净灵通，周流三界。千变万化，统摄阴阳。体用真常，无穷极矣。观彼孤魂，深宜哀愍。此奉太宗圣命：选集诸僧，参禅讲法。大开方便门庭，广运慈悲舟楫，普济苦海群生，脱免沉疴六趣。引归真路，普玩鸿蒙；动止无为，混成纯素。仗此良因，邀赏清都绛阙；乘吾胜会，脱离地狱凡笼。早登极乐任逍遥，来往西方随自在。诗曰：一炉永寿香，几卷超生箓。无边妙法宣，无际天恩沐。冤孽尽消除，孤魂皆出狱。愿保我邦家，清平万年福。”太宗看了满心欢喜，对众僧道：“汝等秉立丹衷，切休怠慢佛事。待后功成完备，各各福有所归，朕当重赏，决不空劳。”那一千二百僧，一齐顿首称谢。
gt_translation: Before and after the thousand official rings are worn, the five guards' flags are lined on both sides. Holding a gourd, holding an axe and a tomahawk, paired with each other; a candle with a red gauze, an incense burner, and a dignified atmosphere. The dragon and the phoenix dance, and the owl recommends the eagle. The holy son is righteous, the loyal minister is good. Jiefu passed Shunyu for thousands of years and leveled Wandai Saiyao Tang. See also the crank umbrella, the rolling dragon robe, and the rays of light; Bead crown jade belt, purple ribbon gold medal. Escort thousands of troops, and support the generals in two lines. The emperor bathed in piety and respected the Buddha, took refuge in the fruit of good deeds, and rejoiced in incense. The king of Tang drove a large car, arrived in front of the temple early, ordered the music horn to stop, got off the chariot, and led many officials. Worship Buddha and incense. The three rounds have been completed, look up and see, there is indeed a good dojo, but you can see: banners are fluttering, and the treasure cover is shining. Flags fluttered and danced, condensed the sky and swayed colorful clouds; Baogai was flying, and the sun was shining and red and electric. The World-Honored Golden Elephant has a splendid appearance, and the Arhat jade is majestic. Vase with immortal flowers, burning sandalwood in the furnace. Immortal flowers are placed in the vase, and the brocade tree is shining brightly in the treasure temple; When the new fruit is built, the red plate is built, and the odd-shaped candy cake is piled up in a colorful case. The eminent monks listed and recited the scriptures, wishing to pull the lonely soul away from suffering. Taizong, both civil and military, took incense, worshipped the Buddha's golden body, and participated in the Arhats. See also the great Chandu Gang, Master Chen Xuanzang, who led the monks to worship the Tang king. After the ceremony, they were divided into classes and settled in their meditation positions. The Master presented Jigu Bangwen and Taizong to read. It is very good. Looking at his lonely soul, it is deeply appropriate to mourn. This is in accordance with Taizong's holy order: to select monks, participate in Zen teaching, and open the door for convenience, transport the boat of compassion, and help people in the sea of suffering. , play Hongmeng in general; move and stop doing nothing, mix it into pure vegetarian. With this good reason, I invite you to reward the Qing capital Jiangque; take advantage of my victory to get out of the cage of hell. Get to the bliss as soon as possible, and travel to and from the West at will. The poem says: 1 Longevity incense in the furnace, several rolls of super-birth urns. Boundless wonderful teachings are proclaimed, and boundless heaven is blessed. All injustices have been eliminated, and all lonely souls have been released from prison. I wish to protect our family and keep the peace and prosperity forever." Taizong was full of joy and said to the monks : "You stand firm, and don't neglect the Buddha's affairs. When your success is complete, and everyone has their own blessings, I will reward them, and I will never work in vain."

human_translations.translator_1: A thousand lords with girdle-jade walk in front and rear. The many flags of guardsmen stand both left and right. Those holding gilt bludgeons, And halberds and axes, March in pairs and pairs; The red silk lanterns, The royal incense urn, Move in solemnity. The dragons fly and the phoenixes dance; The falcons soar and the eagles take wing. This Son of Heaven’s an upright sage; The righteous ministers are good. They increase our bliss by a thousand years, surpassing Yu and Shun; They secure peace of ten thousand ages, rivaling Yao and Tang. We also see the curve-handled umbrella, And robes with rolling dragons— Their glare lighting up each other; The jade joined-rings, The phoenix fans, Waving through holy mist. Those caps of pearls and belts of jade; The purple sashes and medals of gold. A thousand rows of soldiers protect the Throne; Two lines of marshals uphold the carriage. This emperor, cleansed and sincere, bows to the Buddha, Glad to raise incense and seek virtue’s fruit. The grand cortege of the Tang emperor soon arrived in front of the temple. The emperor ordered a halt to the music, left the carriages, and led many officials in the worship of Buddha by taking up burning incense sticks in their hands. After bowing three times holding the incense, they raised their heads and looked around them. This was indeed a splendid religious hall. You see Dancing flags and banners; Bright, gleaming sunshades. Dancing flags and banners Fill the air with strands of flashing colored mists. Bright, gleaming sunshades Glow in the sun as fiery bolts. Imposing, the gold image of Lokājyeṣṭha;14 Most awesome, the jade features of the arhats. Divine flowers fill the vases. Sandalwood incense burn in the urns. The divine flowers filling the vases Adorn the temple with a brilliant forest of brocade. The sandalwood incense burning in the urns Covers the clear sky with waves of fragrant clouds. Piled high on red trays are fruits in season. On colored counters, mounds of cakes and sweets rest. Rows of noble priests chant the holy sūtras To save from their travails those orphaned souls. Taizong and his officials each lifted the incense; they also worshipped the golden body of the Buddha and paid homage to the arhats. Thereafter, the Master of the Law, Chen Xuanzang, the Grand Expositor of the Faith, led the various monks to greet the Tang emperor. After the ceremony, they went back to their seats according to their rank and station. The priest then presented Taizong with the proclamation for the deliverance of the orphaned souls. It read: The supreme virtue is vast and endless, for Buddhism is founded upon Nirvāṇa. The spirit of the pure and the clean circulates freely and flows everywhere in the Three Regions. There are a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, all regulated by the forces of yin and yang. Boundless and vast indeed are the substance, the function, the true nature, and the permanence of such phenomena. But look at those orphaned souls, how worthy they are of our pity and commiseration! Now by the holy command of Taizong, we have selected and assembled various priests, who will engage in meditation and in the proclamation of the Law. Flinging wide the gates of salvation and setting in motion many vessels of mercy, we would deliver you, the multitudes, from the Sea of Woe and save you from perdition and from the Sixfold Path. You will be led to return to the way of truth and to enjoy the bliss of Heaven. Whether it be by motion, rest, or nonactivity, you will be united with, and become, pure essences. Therefore make use of this noble occasion, for you are invited to the pleasures of the celestial city. Take advantage of our Grand Mass so that you may find release from Hell’s confinement, ascend quickly and freely to ultimate bliss, and travel without restraint in the Region of the West.15 The poem says: An urn of immortal incense. Some scrolls of salvific power. As we proclaim this boundless Law, Receive now Heaven’s endless grace. All your guilt and crime abolished, You lost souls may leave your prison. May our nation be firmly blessed With peace long and all-embracing. Highly pleased by what he read, Taizong said to the monks, “Be firm, all of you, in your devotion, and do not slack in your service to Buddha. After the achievement of merit and after each has received his blessing, we shall reward you handsomely. Be assured that you will not have labored in vain.”
human_translations.translator_2: There was no thunder and no lightning after this. This made the Wizard still more anxious, and he burnt more incense and charms and recited more incantations and struck the table as his fourth signal. Instantly the dragons from the four oceans appeared. Sun cried out above their heads, “Aoguang, where do you think you are going?” Aoguang and his companions came forward and bowed. Then Sun told them what he had told the other helpers before, and added, “You helped me before though not successfully. Today I hope you will help me with success.” The Dragon King replied, “I gladly obey your orders.” Sun said, “I beg of you to give me a helping hand. The Wizard’s signal of the fourth performance is now finished. It is now my turn, and I expect you all to help me. I burn no incense and have no signal but my club. When I lift up my spear the first time, I want the wind to blow.” The Mistress of the Wind said, “The wind shall blow.” “When I lift up my spear the second time, I want the clouds to gather.” The Master of the Clouds said, “The clouds shall gather.” “When I lift up my spear the third time, I want thunder and lightning.” The Master of Thunder and Mistress of Lightning said, “You shall have them in abundance.” “When I lift up my spear the fourth time, I want rain.” The Dragon replied, “Your orders shall be obeyed.” “When I lift up my spear the fifth time, I want a clear sky without fail.” Having arranged this, he restored the false Sun and took his place. He shouted out, “Master Wizard, your fourth signal for performance is now over and there has been neither wind, clouds, thunder, lightning, nor rain. Now it is my time to try.” The Wizard came down from his platform altar and went to the gallery by the king, and the Monkey followed him. The king asked the wizard how it was that none of his four attempts were successful. The wizard replied, “The rain king was not at home today.” The Monkey angrily replied, “The dragon gods were all at home, but your Royal Wizard is not sufficiently skilful.” The king then ordered the Buddhist monks to mount the platform. Sun invited the Master to go, but he said he could not command rain.
human_translations.translator_3: “How wonderful!” gasped all present—including the emperor—kneeling, bowing, and burning incense. Taizong called quickly for a skilled painter to sketch a true likeness of the Bodhisattva, but as soon as the artist lifted his brush, the vision vaporized, leaving only a slip of paper drifting down on the breeze. On it was written the following message: Greetings, Emperor of the Tang! 108,000 miles west of here, wonderful texts speak of the Mahayana. Once distributed throughout your empire, these sutras will deliver the ghosts of the damned from Hell. He who is willing to seek them will become a golden Buddha. “Let’s pause the mass and our pursuit of virtue until someone has brought back these miraculous scriptures,” decided the emperor. “But who will go?” asked his officials. “Though entirely useless,” Xuanzang instantly spoke up, “I volunteer to fetch these treasures that will secure the empire in perpetuity.” The emperor immediately raised Xuanzang to his feet and bowed four times to him. “For such sacrifice and service, we will become brothers.” “I swear on my life to reach the Western Heaven,” Xuanzang responded, overwhelmed. “If not, I will never return home and instead pass straight to Hell.” The beaming emperor now returned to the palace, to prepare Xuanzang’s travel documents and await an auspicious day for his departure. Xuanzang, meanwhile, went back to his own temple, which was buzzing with the news of his pledge. “Did you really volunteer to go to the Western Heaven?” one of his disciples asked him. “The way is full of tigers, leopards, demons, and monsters, wide rivers and high mountains. Will we ever see you again?” “I have made a solemn oath,” said Xuanzang. “I must repay the emperor’s generosity by serving the country. If I fail, I will be damned to eternal perdition. Remember: The active mind conjures up demons; the stilled mind extinguishes them. I may be gone for two, three, seven years, or forever. But if the pine tree inside our gate points eastward, you’ll know that I’ll be back soon.” The next morning at court, Taizong wrote out a document describing the mission and stamped it with an imperial seal granting free passage to its bearer. “The stars are auspiciously aligned today for the start of a long journey,” the Department of Astronomy reported.
human_translations.translator_4: A thousand officials with jade at their belts walked in due order. The banners of the five guards are drawn up on either side. Holding golden gourds, Wielding battle-axes, They stand in pairs; Lamps of purple gauze, Imperial censers, Make majestic clouds. Dragons fly and phoenixes dance, Ospreys and eagles soar. True is the enlightened Son of Heaven, Good are his just and loyal ministers. This age of prosperity surpasses the time of Shun and Yu; The eternal peace he has given outdoes that of Yao and Tang. Under a parasol with curved handle The dragon robe sweeps in, Dazzling bright. Interlocking jade rings, Coloured phoenix fans, Shimmer with a magic glow. Pearl crowns and belts of jade, Gold seals on purple cords. A thousand regiments of soldiers protect the imperial chariot, Two lines of generals carry the royal chair. Bathed and reverent, the Emperor comes to worship the Buddha, Submitting to the True Achievement as he joyfully burns incense. When the carriage of the Tang Emperor reached the temple, orders were given to stop the music as he descended from the vehicle and went at the head of his officials to bow to the Buddha and burn incense. When he had done this three times he looked up and saw what a magnificent assembly it was: Dancing banners, Flying canopies. When the banners danced The sky shook with the clouds of silk; When the canopies flew The sun gleamed as the red lightning flashed. Perfect the image of the statue of the Honoured One, Mighty the grandeur of the Arhats' countenances. Magic flowers in a vase, Censers burning sandalwood and laka. As the fairy flowers stand in vases Trees like brocade fill the temple with their brightness. As the censers burn sandalwood and laka Clouds of incense rise to the azure heaven. Fresh fruit of the season is piled in vermilion dishes, Exotic sweets are heaped on the silk-covered tables. Serried ranks of holy monks intone the surras To save abandoned souls from suffering. Taizong and his civil and military officials all burned incense, bowed to the golden body of the Lord Buddha, and paid their respects to the Arhats. The Hierarch Chen Xuanzang then led all the monks to bow to the Emperor, and when this was over they divided into their groups and went to their meditation places while the Hierarch showed the Emperor the notice about the delivery of the lonely ghosts. It read: “Mysterious is the ultimate virtue, and the Sect of Meditation leads to Nirvana. The purity of the truth is all-knowing; it pervades the Three Regions of the universe. Through its countless changes it controls the Negative and Positive; unbounded are the embodiments of the eternal reality. In considering those forlorn ghosts one should be deeply distressed. At the sacred command of Taizong we have assembled some chosen monks for meditation and preaching. He has opened wide the gates of enlightenment and rowed far the boat of mercy, saving all the beings in the sea of suffering, and delivering those who had long been afflicted by the six ways of existence. They will be led back to the right road and revel in the great chaos; in action and in passivity they will be at one with primal simplicity. For this wonderful cause they are invited to see the purple gates of the pure capital, and through our assembly they will escape from the confines of Hell to climb to the World of Bliss and be free, wandering as they please in the Paradise of the West. As the poem goes: A burner of incense of longevity, A few spells to achieve rebirth. The infinite Law is proclaimed, The boundless mercy of Heaven is shown. When sins are all washed away, The neglected souls leave Hell. We pray to protect our country; May it stay at peace and be blessed.” When he had read this the Tang Emperor's heart was filled with happiness and he said to the monks, “Hold firm to your sincerity and never allow yourselves a moment's slackness in the service of the Buddha. Later on, when the Assembly is over, you will be blessed and we shall richly reward you. You shall certainly not have labored in vain.” The twelve hundred monks all kowtowed to thank him.

translation:
Thousand officials surrounded the Emperor, their emblems fanning out before and behind. The guards stood in rows on either side, swords and axes gleaming, in pairs facing each other.  Red silk candles flickered, while incense burned in ornate censers, filling the hall with a rich, palpable fragrance. Dragons soared and phoenixes took flight, as eagles and falcons spread their wings. The divinely appointed Son of Heaven, the Emperor, sat upright, surrounded by loyal and righteous ministers. His virtues have surpassed those of Shun and Yu from a thousand years past, his rule will rival that of Yao and Tang, bringing prosperity for ten thousand generations.

A sight to behold! The jeweled handles of the parasols and the embroidered dragon robes shimmered, their light reflected in the jade ornaments and colorful peacock fans that rippled in the breeze. Crowned in jewels, adorned with jade belts and purple sashes, he was escorted by thousands of imperial guards and a line of dignitaries. The Emperor bathed in the devotion of these holy offerings, bowing in piety as he held the incense and worshipped.

The Tang King arrived early, arriving before the temple gates. He silenced the music, disembarked from his palanquin, and led a procession of officials. He too, bowed and held incense as he worshipped the Buddha, circling the altar three times. Then, raising his gaze, he beheld the magnificent sight before him: banners fluttered in the wind, and the jeweled canopy shone brightly. 

The banners danced, painted with rainbows across the sky; the canopy shimmered, reflecting the sun in a cascade of vibrant light. The image of the Buddha, majestic in his golden form, sat serenely alongside the Arhats, their jade faces radiating power.  Flowers in vases decorated the hall, and sandalwood incense perfumed the air.  The incense filled the room, its fragrant smoke reaching through the highest heavens. A platter of fresh fruits and delicate pastries adorned with sugar candy lay ready on a colorful table.

The high monks stood in a row, chanting the sacred scriptures, hoping to free the souls from their suffering. The Emperor, both civil and military officials, each lit incense and bowed to the Buddha's golden image, paying homage to the Arhats. 

Then, Master Xuanzang, chief abbot of the Grand Trinities Monastery, led the assembled monks in a bow before the Tang King. After the ceremony concluded, the monks returned to their meditation positions, and Xuanzang presented the Emperor with a scroll titled "The List for Liberating Souls," saying, "By the benevolence of Heaven, we have the path of Zen. Its purity and insight transcends the three realms. It embraces all transformations, uniting yin and yang. Its essence is true and eternal, infinite in its power. Observing these lonely souls, one must feel compassion. Thus, by command of the Emperor, we have gathered the monks to practice meditation and preach the Dharma. With open doors, we extend our compassionate embrace, offering salvation to all beings suffering in the sea of existence. We lead them to liberation from their mortal ailments, guiding them to the True Way, transcending the veil of illusion. By mastering stillness and movement, they achieve pure emptiness, free from all attachments.

Following this auspicious occasion, we celebrate the grandeur of the capital city, a shining beacon of civilization. Grasping this precious opportunity, we overcome the confines of the underworld and ascend to bliss. Soaring freely in the realm of Ultimate Happiness, we move back and forth freely,  free from the Western Pure Land. Poetry says:

One incense burner, a fragrance for eternal life,
A scroll of transcendent scriptures.
Infinite magical laws are proclaimed,
Unending heavenly grace pervades.

Every grievance is erased,
Each soul is freed from its prison.
May our kingdom prosper for ten thousand years,
Enjoy peace and tranquility.

The Emperor, overjoyed, addressed the assembled monks: "You hold true devotion in your hearts. Never neglect the practice of Buddhist teachings. When your efforts bear fruit and your aspirations are fulfilled, I shall reward you generously. I vow that your labor will not be in vain."

The 1,200 monks bowed in unison, expressing their gratitude.
source_text: 千官环佩分前后，五卫旌旗列两旁。执金瓜，擎斧钺，双双对对；绛纱烛，御炉香，霭霭堂堂。龙飞凤舞，鹗荐鹰扬。圣明天子正，忠义大臣良。介福千年过舜禹，升平万代赛尧汤。又见那曲柄伞，滚龙袍，辉光相射；玉连环，彩凤扇，瑞霭飘扬。珠冠玉带，紫绶金章。护驾军千队，扶舆将两行。这皇帝沐浴虔诚尊敬佛，皈依善果喜拈香。唐王大驾，早到寺前，吩咐住了音乐响器，下了车辇，引着多官。拜佛拈香。三匝已毕，抬头观看，果然好座道场，但见：幢幡飘舞，宝盖飞辉。幢幡飘舞，凝空道道彩霞摇；宝盖飞辉，映日翩翩红电彻。世尊金象貌臻臻，罗汉玉容威烈烈。瓶插仙花，炉焚檀降。瓶插仙花，锦树辉辉漫宝刹；炉焚檀降，香云霭霭透清霄。时新果品砌朱盘，奇样糖酥堆彩案。高僧罗列诵真经，愿拔孤魂离苦难。太宗文武俱各拈香，拜了佛祖金身，参了罗汉。又见那大阐都纲陈玄奘法师引众僧罗拜唐王。礼毕，分班各安禅位，法师献上济孤榜文与太宗看，榜曰：“至德渺茫，禅宗寂灭。清净灵通，周流三界。千变万化，统摄阴阳。体用真常，无穷极矣。观彼孤魂，深宜哀愍。此奉太宗圣命：选集诸僧，参禅讲法。大开方便门庭，广运慈悲舟楫，普济苦海群生，脱免沉疴六趣。引归真路，普玩鸿蒙；动止无为，混成纯素。仗此良因，邀赏清都绛阙；乘吾胜会，脱离地狱凡笼。早登极乐任逍遥，来往西方随自在。诗曰：一炉永寿香，几卷超生箓。无边妙法宣，无际天恩沐。冤孽尽消除，孤魂皆出狱。愿保我邦家，清平万年福。”太宗看了满心欢喜，对众僧道：“汝等秉立丹衷，切休怠慢佛事。待后功成完备，各各福有所归，朕当重赏，决不空劳。”那一千二百僧，一齐顿首称谢。

human_translations.translator_2: There was no thunder and no lightning after this. He shouted out, “Master Wizard, your fourth signal for performance is now over and there has been neither wind, clouds, thunder, lightning, nor rain. Sun invited the Master to go, but he said he could not command rain.
human_translations.translator_3: “How wonderful!” gasped all present—including the emperor—kneeling, bowing, and burning incense. Taizong called quickly for a skilled painter to sketch a true likeness of the Bodhisattva, but as soon as the artist lifted his brush, the vision vaporized, leaving only a slip of paper drifting down on the breeze. On it was written the following message: Greetings, Emperor of the Tang! 108,000 miles west of here, wonderful texts speak of the Mahayana. Once distributed throughout your empire, these sutras will deliver the ghosts of the damned from Hell. He who is willing to seek them will become a golden Buddha. “Let’s pause the mass and our pursuit of virtue until someone has brought back these miraculous scriptures,” decided the emperor. “But who will go?” asked his officials. “Though entirely useless,” Xuanzang instantly spoke up, “I volunteer to fetch these treasures that will secure the empire in perpetuity.” The emperor immediately raised Xuanzang to his feet and bowed four times to him. “For such sacrifice and service, we will become brothers.” “I swear on my life to reach the Western Heaven,” Xuanzang responded, overwhelmed. “If not, I will never return home and instead pass straight to Hell.” The beaming emperor now returned to the palace, to prepare Xuanzang’s travel documents and await an auspicious day for his departure. Xuanzang, meanwhile, went back to his own temple, which was buzzing with the news of his pledge. “Did you really volunteer to go to the Western Heaven?” one of his disciples asked him. “The way is full of tigers, leopards, demons, and monsters, wide rivers and high mountains. Will we ever see you again?” “I have made a solemn oath,” said Xuanzang. “I must repay the emperor’s generosity by serving the country. If I fail, I will be damned to eternal perdition. Remember: The active mind conjures up demons; the stilled mind extinguishes them. I may be gone for two, three, seven years, or forever. But if the pine tree inside our gate points eastward, you’ll know that I’ll be back soon.” The next morning at court, Taizong wrote out a document describing the mission and stamped it with an imperial seal granting free passage to its bearer. “The stars are auspiciously aligned today for the start of a long journey,” the Department of Astronomy reported.

translation:
Thousands of officials flanked the imperial procession, the five guards stood with their banners on either side.  They held golden gourds, axes, and halberds, facing each other in pairs; the red silk candles and incense burner filled the air with a sweet fragrance. Dragons danced and phoenixes soared, eagles took to the sky, hawks rising in pursuit.  The august emperor, a righteous and virtuous ruler, surpassed even Shun and Yu of old, his reign of peace would rival that of Yao and Tang.   Then came the sight of the curved-handle umbrella, the dragon-robed emperor, the light of the jewels reflecting; jade ornaments, and colored phoenix fans, auspicious clouds billowed around him.  Jewelled crowns, jade belts, purple sashes, and golden emblems adorned him.  Thousands of soldiers formed a protective escort, two rows of palanquins carried him. This emperor, bathed in a reverent devotion, respectfully bowed to Buddha, accepting the blessings of good fortune, offering incense. 
The Tang King arrived early, came before the temple, silenced the music and instruments, stepped out of his carriage, followed by many officials. He bowed, and offered incense before Buddha. After three circumambulations, he looked up and saw a truly magnificent gathering. Banners swayed in the wind, precious banners shone brightly. The banners danced and swayed,  casting dancing rainbows upon the sky; the banners shone, reflecting the sun, lightning flashed red.  The statue of the World-Honored One, with its majestic elephant-like appearance,  and the bodhisattvas with their serene and powerful faces stood majestically. Flowers were arranged in bottles, and sandalwood was burned, incense fragrance permeated the air. Bottles holding fragrant flowers, and jeweled trees glistened throughout the sacred temple; sandalwood burned, the fragrant smoke drifted through the clear sky.  Fresh fruit was arranged on trays, exotic sweets piled high on colorful tables. High monks recited the true scriptures, praying to free lonely souls from suffering. The emperor, both in civil and military attire, each offered incense, bowed before the Buddha's golden body, and paid respects to the bodhisattvas. 
Then, the eminent Master Xuanzang, master of the Great Teaching of the Dharma, led the congregation of monks and nuns to bow to the Tang King.  After the ceremony, each monk found their designated meditation spot. The master presented the "Jùgū Biǎng," a scroll with a proclamation, to the emperor.  The scroll declared: "Compassionate virtues are immeasurable, the Zen sect is eternal. Pure and clear understanding flows through the three realms. Thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, encompassing yin and yang. Its essence is true and unchanging, infinite and limitless. Consider the unfortunate souls, they should be deeply pitied. By imperial decree: we gather monks and nuns to practice Chan, to teach the Dharma, open wide the gates of convenience, set sail on the vast ocean of compassion, to save all living beings in the sea of suffering, and free them from illness and rebirth.  Guide them to the true path, liberate them from the confusion of chaos; inaction, yet moving, purity arises.  Depending on this opportunity, enjoy the blessings of the clear capital and magnificent palaces;  take advantage of this favorable gathering, break free from the prison of the realms of desire, quickly attain bliss, travel freely to the West, enjoy ultimate freedom. The poem says:  A single incense burner, eternal life; a few scrolls, rebirth guaranteed. Infinite wonders of the Dharma are proclaimed, boundless grace of heaven is received.  All karmic debts are eradicated, all tormented souls are liberated. May my empire prosper, enjoy eternal peace and happiness." The emperor, after reading, was filled with joy and said to the monks: "Your sincerity is deeply appreciated, do not slacken in your devotion to the Buddha. After your meritorious deeds are accomplished, and when all are fulfilled, I shall bestow great rewards, you will not labor in vain."  The one thousand two hundred monks, in unison, bowed their heads and thanked him.
source_text: 千官环佩分前后，五卫旌旗列两旁。执金瓜，擎斧钺，双双对对；绛纱烛，御炉香，霭霭堂堂。龙飞凤舞，鹗荐鹰扬。圣明天子正，忠义大臣良。介福千年过舜禹，升平万代赛尧汤。又见那曲柄伞，滚龙袍，辉光相射；玉连环，彩凤扇，瑞霭飘扬。珠冠玉带，紫绶金章。护驾军千队，扶舆将两行。这皇帝沐浴虔诚尊敬佛，皈依善果喜拈香。唐王大驾，早到寺前，吩咐住了音乐响器，下了车辇，引着多官。拜佛拈香。三匝已毕，抬头观看，果然好座道场，但见：幢幡飘舞，宝盖飞辉。幢幡飘舞，凝空道道彩霞摇；宝盖飞辉，映日翩翩红电彻。世尊金象貌臻臻，罗汉玉容威烈烈。瓶插仙花，炉焚檀降。瓶插仙花，锦树辉辉漫宝刹；炉焚檀降，香云霭霭透清霄。时新果品砌朱盘，奇样糖酥堆彩案。高僧罗列诵真经，愿拔孤魂离苦难。太宗文武俱各拈香，拜了佛祖金身，参了罗汉。又见那大阐都纲陈玄奘法师引众僧罗拜唐王。礼毕，分班各安禅位，法师献上济孤榜文与太宗看，榜曰：“至德渺茫，禅宗寂灭。清净灵通，周流三界。千变万化，统摄阴阳。体用真常，无穷极矣。观彼孤魂，深宜哀愍。此奉太宗圣命：选集诸僧，参禅讲法。大开方便门庭，广运慈悲舟楫，普济苦海群生，脱免沉疴六趣。引归真路，普玩鸿蒙；动止无为，混成纯素。仗此良因，邀赏清都绛阙；乘吾胜会，脱离地狱凡笼。早登极乐任逍遥，来往西方随自在。诗曰：一炉永寿香，几卷超生箓。无边妙法宣，无际天恩沐。冤孽尽消除，孤魂皆出狱。愿保我邦家，清平万年福。”太宗看了满心欢喜，对众僧道：“汝等秉立丹衷，切休怠慢佛事。待后功成完备，各各福有所归，朕当重赏，决不空劳。”那一千二百僧，一齐顿首称谢。

Holding a gourd, holding an axe and a tomahawk, paired with each other; a candle with a red gauze, an incense burner, and a dignified atmosphere. The dragon and the phoenix dance, and the owl recommends the eagle. The holy son is righteous, the loyal minister is good. Jiefu passed Shunyu for thousands of years and leveled Wandai Saiyao Tang. See also the crank umbrella, the rolling dragon robe, and the rays of light; Bead crown jade belt, purple ribbon gold medal. Escort thousands of troops, and support the generals in two lines. The three rounds have been completed, look up and see, there is indeed a good dojo, but you can see: banners are fluttering, and the treasure cover is shining. Flags fluttered and danced, condensed the sky and swayed colorful clouds; Baogai was flying, and the sun was shining and red and electric. The World-Honored Golden Elephant has a splendid appearance, and the Arhat jade is majestic. Vase with immortal flowers, burning sandalwood in the furnace. Immortal flowers are placed in the vase, and the brocade tree is shining brightly in the treasure temple; When the new fruit is built, the red plate is built, and the odd-shaped candy cake is piled up in a colorful case. The eminent monks listed and recited the scriptures, wishing to pull the lonely soul away from suffering. Taizong, both civil and military, took incense, worshipped the Buddha's golden body, and participated in the Arhats. See also the great Chandu Gang, Master Chen Xuanzang, who led the monks to worship the Tang king. After the ceremony, they were divided into classes and settled in their meditation positions. The Master presented Jigu Bangwen and Taizong to read. It is very good. Looking at his lonely soul, it is deeply appropriate to mourn. This is in accordance with Taizong's holy order: to select monks, participate in Zen teaching, and open the door for convenience, transport the boat of compassion, and help people in the sea of suffering. , play Hongmeng in general; move and stop doing nothing, mix it into pure vegetarian. With this good reason, I invite you to reward the Qing capital Jiangque; take advantage of my victory to get out of the cage of hell. Get to the bliss as soon as possible, and travel to and from the West at will. The poem says: 1 Longevity incense in the furnace, several rolls of super-birth urns. Boundless wonderful teachings are proclaimed, and boundless heaven is blessed. All injustices have been eliminated, and all lonely souls have been released from prison. I wish to protect our family and keep the peace and prosperity forever." Taizong was full of joy and said to the monks : "You stand firm, and don't neglect the Buddha's affairs. When your success is complete, and everyone has their own blessings, I will reward them, and I will never work in vain."

human_translations.translator_1: A thousand lords with girdle-jade walk in front and rear. The many flags of guardsmen stand both left and right. Those holding gilt bludgeons, And halberds and axes, March in pairs and pairs; The red silk lanterns, The royal incense urn, Move in solemnity. The dragons fly and the phoenixes dance; The falcons soar and the eagles take wing. This Son of Heaven’s an upright sage; The righteous ministers are good. They increase our bliss by a thousand years, surpassing Yu and Shun; They secure peace of ten thousand ages, rivaling Yao and Tang. We also see the curve-handled umbrella, And robes with rolling dragons— Their glare lighting up each other; The jade joined-rings, The phoenix fans, Waving through holy mist. Those caps of pearls and belts of jade; The purple sashes and medals of gold. A thousand rows of soldiers protect the Throne; Two lines of marshals uphold the carriage. This emperor, cleansed and sincere, bows to the Buddha, Glad to raise incense and seek virtue’s fruit. The grand cortege of the Tang emperor soon arrived in front of the temple. The emperor ordered a halt to the music, left the carriages, and led many officials in the worship of Buddha by taking up burning incense sticks in their hands. After bowing three times holding the incense, they raised their heads and looked around them. This was indeed a splendid religious hall. You see Dancing flags and banners; Bright, gleaming sunshades. Dancing flags and banners Fill the air with strands of flashing colored mists. Bright, gleaming sunshades Glow in the sun as fiery bolts. Imposing, the gold image of Lokājyeṣṭha;14 Most awesome, the jade features of the arhats. Divine flowers fill the vases. Sandalwood incense burn in the urns. The divine flowers filling the vases Adorn the temple with a brilliant forest of brocade. The sandalwood incense burning in the urns Covers the clear sky with waves of fragrant clouds. Piled high on red trays are fruits in season. On colored counters, mounds of cakes and sweets rest. Rows of noble priests chant the holy sūtras To save from their travails those orphaned souls. Taizong and his officials each lifted the incense; they also worshipped the golden body of the Buddha and paid homage to the arhats. Thereafter, the Master of the Law, Chen Xuanzang, the Grand Expositor of the Faith, led the various monks to greet the Tang emperor. After the ceremony, they went back to their seats according to their rank and station. The priest then presented Taizong with the proclamation for the deliverance of the orphaned souls. It read: The supreme virtue is vast and endless, for Buddhism is founded upon Nirvāṇa. The spirit of the pure and the clean circulates freely and flows everywhere in the Three Regions. There are a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, all regulated by the forces of yin and yang. Boundless and vast indeed are the substance, the function, the true nature, and the permanence of such phenomena. But look at those orphaned souls, how worthy they are of our pity and commiseration! Now by the holy command of Taizong, we have selected and assembled various priests, who will engage in meditation and in the proclamation of the Law. Flinging wide the gates of salvation and setting in motion many vessels of mercy, we would deliver you, the multitudes, from the Sea of Woe and save you from perdition and from the Sixfold Path. You will be led to return to the way of truth and to enjoy the bliss of Heaven. Whether it be by motion, rest, or nonactivity, you will be united with, and become, pure essences. Therefore make use of this noble occasion, for you are invited to the pleasures of the celestial city. Take advantage of our Grand Mass so that you may find release from Hell’s confinement, ascend quickly and freely to ultimate bliss, and travel without restraint in the Region of the West.15 The poem says: An urn of immortal incense. Some scrolls of salvific power. As we proclaim this boundless Law, Receive now Heaven’s endless grace. All your guilt and crime abolished, You lost souls may leave your prison. May our nation be firmly blessed With peace long and all-embracing. Highly pleased by what he read, Taizong said to the monks, “Be firm, all of you, in your devotion, and do not slack in your service to Buddha. After the achievement of merit and after each has received his blessing, we shall reward you handsomely. Be assured that you will not have labored in vain.”
human_translations.translator_2: There was no thunder and no lightning after this. This made the Wizard still more anxious, and he burnt more incense and charms and recited more incantations and struck the table as his fourth signal. Instantly the dragons from the four oceans appeared. Sun cried out above their heads, “Aoguang, where do you think you are going?” Aoguang and his companions came forward and bowed. Then Sun told them what he had told the other helpers before, and added, “You helped me before though not successfully. Today I hope you will help me with success.” The Dragon King replied, “I gladly obey your orders.” Sun said, “I beg of you to give me a helping hand. The Wizard’s signal of the fourth performance is now finished. It is now my turn, and I expect you all to help me. I burn no incense and have no signal but my club. When I lift up my spear the first time, I want the wind to blow.” The Mistress of the Wind said, “The wind shall blow.” “When I lift up my spear the second time, I want the clouds to gather.” The Master of the Clouds said, “The clouds shall gather.” “When I lift up my spear the third time, I want thunder and lightning.” The Master of Thunder and Mistress of Lightning said, “You shall have them in abundance.” “When I lift up my spear the fourth time, I want rain.” The Dragon replied, “Your orders shall be obeyed.” “When I lift up my spear the fifth time, I want a clear sky without fail.” Having arranged this, he restored the false Sun and took his place. He shouted out, “Master Wizard, your fourth signal for performance is now over and there has been neither wind, clouds, thunder, lightning, nor rain. Now it is my time to try.” The Wizard came down from his platform altar and went to the gallery by the king, and the Monkey followed him. The king asked the wizard how it was that none of his four attempts were successful. The wizard replied, “The rain king was not at home today.” The Monkey angrily replied, “The dragon gods were all at home, but your Royal Wizard is not sufficiently skilful.” The king then ordered the Buddhist monks to mount the platform. Sun invited the Master to go, but he said he could not command rain.
human_translations.translator_3: “How wonderful!” gasped all present—including the emperor—kneeling, bowing, and burning incense. Taizong called quickly for a skilled painter to sketch a true likeness of the Bodhisattva, but as soon as the artist lifted his brush, the vision vaporized, leaving only a slip of paper drifting down on the breeze. On it was written the following message: Greetings, Emperor of the Tang! 108,000 miles west of here, wonderful texts speak of the Mahayana. Once distributed throughout your empire, these sutras will deliver the ghosts of the damned from Hell. He who is willing to seek them will become a golden Buddha. “Let’s pause the mass and our pursuit of virtue until someone has brought back these miraculous scriptures,” decided the emperor. “But who will go?” asked his officials. “Though entirely useless,” Xuanzang instantly spoke up, “I volunteer to fetch these treasures that will secure the empire in perpetuity.” The emperor immediately raised Xuanzang to his feet and bowed four times to him. “For such sacrifice and service, we will become brothers.” “I swear on my life to reach the Western Heaven,” Xuanzang responded, overwhelmed. “If not, I will never return home and instead pass straight to Hell.” The beaming emperor now returned to the palace, to prepare Xuanzang’s travel documents and await an auspicious day for his departure. Xuanzang, meanwhile, went back to his own temple, which was buzzing with the news of his pledge. “Did you really volunteer to go to the Western Heaven?” one of his disciples asked him. “The way is full of tigers, leopards, demons, and monsters, wide rivers and high mountains. Will we ever see you again?” “I have made a solemn oath,” said Xuanzang. “I must repay the emperor’s generosity by serving the country. If I fail, I will be damned to eternal perdition. Remember: The active mind conjures up demons; the stilled mind extinguishes them. I may be gone for two, three, seven years, or forever. But if the pine tree inside our gate points eastward, you’ll know that I’ll be back soon.” The next morning at court, Taizong wrote out a document describing the mission and stamped it with an imperial seal granting free passage to its bearer. “The stars are auspiciously aligned today for the start of a long journey,” the Department of Astronomy reported.
human_translations.translator_4: A thousand officials with jade at their belts walked in due order. The banners of the five guards are drawn up on either side. Holding golden gourds, Wielding battle-axes, They stand in pairs; Lamps of purple gauze, Imperial censers, Make majestic clouds. Dragons fly and phoenixes dance, Ospreys and eagles soar. True is the enlightened Son of Heaven, Good are his just and loyal ministers. This age of prosperity surpasses the time of Shun and Yu; The eternal peace he has given outdoes that of Yao and Tang. Under a parasol with curved handle The dragon robe sweeps in, Dazzling bright. Interlocking jade rings, Coloured phoenix fans, Shimmer with a magic glow. Pearl crowns and belts of jade, Gold seals on purple cords. A thousand regiments of soldiers protect the imperial chariot, Two lines of generals carry the royal chair. Bathed and reverent, the Emperor comes to worship the Buddha, Submitting to the True Achievement as he joyfully burns incense. When the carriage of the Tang Emperor reached the temple, orders were given to stop the music as he descended from the vehicle and went at the head of his officials to bow to the Buddha and burn incense. When he had done this three times he looked up and saw what a magnificent assembly it was: Dancing banners, Flying canopies. When the banners danced The sky shook with the clouds of silk; When the canopies flew The sun gleamed as the red lightning flashed. Perfect the image of the statue of the Honoured One, Mighty the grandeur of the Arhats' countenances. Magic flowers in a vase, Censers burning sandalwood and laka. As the fairy flowers stand in vases Trees like brocade fill the temple with their brightness. As the censers burn sandalwood and laka Clouds of incense rise to the azure heaven. Fresh fruit of the season is piled in vermilion dishes, Exotic sweets are heaped on the silk-covered tables. Serried ranks of holy monks intone the surras To save abandoned souls from suffering. Taizong and his civil and military officials all burned incense, bowed to the golden body of the Lord Buddha, and paid their respects to the Arhats. The Hierarch Chen Xuanzang then led all the monks to bow to the Emperor, and when this was over they divided into their groups and went to their meditation places while the Hierarch showed the Emperor the notice about the delivery of the lonely ghosts. It read: “Mysterious is the ultimate virtue, and the Sect of Meditation leads to Nirvana. The purity of the truth is all-knowing; it pervades the Three Regions of the universe. Through its countless changes it controls the Negative and Positive; unbounded are the embodiments of the eternal reality. In considering those forlorn ghosts one should be deeply distressed. At the sacred command of Taizong we have assembled some chosen monks for meditation and preaching. He has opened wide the gates of enlightenment and rowed far the boat of mercy, saving all the beings in the sea of suffering, and delivering those who had long been afflicted by the six ways of existence. They will be led back to the right road and revel in the great chaos; in action and in passivity they will be at one with primal simplicity. For this wonderful cause they are invited to see the purple gates of the pure capital, and through our assembly they will escape from the confines of Hell to climb to the World of Bliss and be free, wandering as they please in the Paradise of the West. As the poem goes: A burner of incense of longevity, A few spells to achieve rebirth. The infinite Law is proclaimed, The boundless mercy of Heaven is shown. When sins are all washed away, The neglected souls leave Hell. We pray to protect our country; May it stay at peace and be blessed.” When he had read this the Tang Emperor's heart was filled with happiness and he said to the monks, “Hold firm to your sincerity and never allow yourselves a moment's slackness in the service of the Buddha. Later on, when the Assembly is over, you will be blessed and we shall richly reward you. You shall certainly not have labored in vain.” The twelve hundred monks all kowtowed to thank him.

translation:
Thousands of officials surrounded the imperial procession, the five armies' banners stood in two lines on either side. Holding golden gourds, brandishing axes and halberds, they stood in pairs; crimson silk candles illuminated the imperial furnace, emitting a fragrant smoke, filling the hall with grandeur. Dragons and phoenixes danced, eagles soared, falcons dived. The emperor, virtuous and upright, was bathed in reverence, loyal ministers stood beside him, their virtues spanning millennia, surpassing even Shun and Yu, their peace and prosperity rivaling Yao and Tang. 

Then there was the curved-handled parasol, the dragons-woven robe, their radiance shining brightly; jade bracelets and colorful phoenix fans, auspicious clouds drifting.  A jewelled crown, jade belt, purple sashes, and golden orders adorned him. A thousand guards protected him, two lines of chariots followed close behind. The emperor, bathing in the devout respect of the Buddha, enshrined himself with good fruits, reverently taking incense.

The Tang king arrived at the temple early, stopping the music and dismounting his carriage, followed by numerous officials. He bowed to the Buddha, received incense, and made three circumambulations. Upon raising his head, he saw that it was indeed a magnificent temple; pennants danced, treasure-encrusted roofs gleamed. Pennants danced, the sky filled with vibrant hues as if painted by the gods; treasure-encrusted roofs reflected the sun, flames of crimson light streaked across the sky. The Buddha, with his golden elephant-like appearance, emanated enlightenment; arhats, with their jade-like faces, exuded righteous majesty. Vases filled with immortal flowers adorned the temple, sandalwood incense burnt, filling the air with a pure fragrance. Precious fruits were arranged on red plates, unique sugar confections piled high on colorful platforms. High monks sat in rows, reciting the scriptures, hoping to liberate lost souls from suffering. 

Emperor Taizong, both civil and military officials, each offered incense and bowed to the Buddha's golden body, paying homage to the arhats. Then, Grandmaster Xuanzang, renowned for expounding Buddhist teachings, led a multitude of monks in bowing to the Tang king. After the ceremony, the monks settled in their designated meditation spots. Grandmaster Xuanzang presented Emperor Taizong with a banner inscribed with “Redemption Through Zen,” which read: “Supreme Virtue Unfathomable, Zen Essence Profound. Pure and Awakened, Circulating Through the Three Realms. Ever-changing and Everlasting, Governing Yin and Yang. Truth, Constant and Limitless, Infinite in Power. Look at these Lost Souls, Their Plight Needs Compassion. By Imperial Decree: Select Monks Assembled, Zen Meditation and Teachings Proclaimed. Opening the Door of Grace, Navigating the Boat of Compassion, Rescuing the Suffering Multitude from the Sea of Samsara, Freeing Them from Suffering and Rebirth. Guiding Them to True Paths, Experiencing the Cosmic Origin; Actionless Stillness, Transforming into Pure Being. Relying on this Auspicious Opportunity, Feasting in the Jade Palace of Our Capital; Riding on This Fortunate Convergence, Escaping the Hellish Cycle of Existence. Early Ascent to Blissful Joy, Freedom to Roam the West, Reunited with Nirvana.”

Emperor Taizong, filled with joy, addressed the monks: “You all possess righteous intentions; do not neglect Buddhist affairs. When your efforts are complete, each of you will find your reward. I will shower you with blessings, ensuring no labor is in vain.” The 1200 monks, with heads bowed, expressed their gratitude.

human_translations.translator_3: “How wonderful!” gasped all present—including the emperor—kneeling, bowing, and burning incense. Taizong called quickly for a skilled painter to sketch a true likeness of the Bodhisattva, but as soon as the artist lifted his brush, the vision vaporized, leaving only a slip of paper drifting down on the breeze. On it was written the following message: Greetings, Emperor of the Tang! 108,000 miles west of here, wonderful texts speak of the Mahayana. Once distributed throughout your empire, these sutras will deliver the ghosts of the damned from Hell. He who is willing to seek them will become a golden Buddha. “Let’s pause the mass and our pursuit of virtue until someone has brought back these miraculous scriptures,” decided the emperor. “But who will go?” asked his officials. “Though entirely useless,” Xuanzang instantly spoke up, “I volunteer to fetch these treasures that will secure the empire in perpetuity.” The emperor immediately raised Xuanzang to his feet and bowed four times to him. “For such sacrifice and service, we will become brothers.” “I swear on my life to reach the Western Heaven,” Xuanzang responded, overwhelmed. “If not, I will never return home and instead pass straight to Hell.” The beaming emperor now returned to the palace, to prepare Xuanzang’s travel documents and await an auspicious day for his departure. Xuanzang, meanwhile, went back to his own temple, which was buzzing with the news of his pledge. “Did you really volunteer to go to the Western Heaven?” one of his disciples asked him. “The way is full of tigers, leopards, demons, and monsters, wide rivers and high mountains. Will we ever see you again?” “I have made a solemn oath,” said Xuanzang. “I must repay the emperor’s generosity by serving the country. If I fail, I will be damned to eternal perdition. Remember: The active mind conjures up demons; the stilled mind extinguishes them. I may be gone for two, three, seven years, or forever. But if the pine tree inside our gate points eastward, you’ll know that I’ll be back soon.” The next morning at court, Taizong wrote out a document describing the mission and stamped it with an imperial seal granting free passage to its bearer. “The stars are auspiciously aligned today for the start of a long journey,” the Department of Astronomy reported.
human_translations.translator_4: A thousand officials with jade at their belts walked in due order. The banners of the five guards are drawn up on either side. Holding golden gourds, Wielding battle-axes, They stand in pairs; Lamps of purple gauze, Imperial censers, Make majestic clouds. Dragons fly and phoenixes dance, Ospreys and eagles soar. True is the enlightened Son of Heaven, Good are his just and loyal ministers. This age of prosperity surpasses the time of Shun and Yu; The eternal peace he has given outdoes that of Yao and Tang. Under a parasol with curved handle The dragon robe sweeps in, Dazzling bright. Interlocking jade rings, Coloured phoenix fans, Shimmer with a magic glow. Pearl crowns and belts of jade, Gold seals on purple cords. A thousand regiments of soldiers protect the imperial chariot, Two lines of generals carry the royal chair. Bathed and reverent, the Emperor comes to worship the Buddha, Submitting to the True Achievement as he joyfully burns incense. When the carriage of the Tang Emperor reached the temple, orders were given to stop the music as he descended from the vehicle and went at the head of his officials to bow to the Buddha and burn incense. When he had done this three times he looked up and saw what a magnificent assembly it was: Dancing banners, Flying canopies. When the banners danced The sky shook with the clouds of silk; When the canopies flew The sun gleamed as the red lightning flashed. Perfect the image of the statue of the Honoured One, Mighty the grandeur of the Arhats' countenances. Magic flowers in a vase, Censers burning sandalwood and laka. As the fairy flowers stand in vases Trees like brocade fill the temple with their brightness. As the censers burn sandalwood and laka Clouds of incense rise to the azure heaven. Fresh fruit of the season is piled in vermilion dishes, Exotic sweets are heaped on the silk-covered tables. Serried ranks of holy monks intone the surras To save abandoned souls from suffering. Taizong and his civil and military officials all burned incense, bowed to the golden body of the Lord Buddha, and paid their respects to the Arhats. The Hierarch Chen Xuanzang then led all the monks to bow to the Emperor, and when this was over they divided into their groups and went to their meditation places while the Hierarch showed the Emperor the notice about the delivery of the lonely ghosts. It read: “Mysterious is the ultimate virtue, and the Sect of Meditation leads to Nirvana. The purity of the truth is all-knowing; it pervades the Three Regions of the universe. Through its countless changes it controls the Negative and Positive; unbounded are the embodiments of the eternal reality. In considering those forlorn ghosts one should be deeply distressed. At the sacred command of Taizong we have assembled some chosen monks for meditation and preaching. He has opened wide the gates of enlightenment and rowed far the boat of mercy, saving all the beings in the sea of suffering, and delivering those who had long been afflicted by the six ways of existence. They will be led back to the right road and revel in the great chaos; in action and in passivity they will be at one with primal simplicity. For this wonderful cause they are invited to see the purple gates of the pure capital, and through our assembly they will escape from the confines of Hell to climb to the World of Bliss and be free, wandering as they please in the Paradise of the West. As the poem goes: A burner of incense of longevity, A few spells to achieve rebirth. The infinite Law is proclaimed, The boundless mercy of Heaven is shown. When sins are all washed away, The neglected souls leave Hell. We pray to protect our country; May it stay at peace and be blessed.” When he had read this the Tang Emperor's heart was filled with happiness and he said to the monks, “Hold firm to your sincerity and never allow yourselves a moment's slackness in the service of the Buddha. Later on, when the Assembly is over, you will be blessed and we shall richly reward you. You shall certainly not have labored in vain.” The twelve hundred monks all kowtowed to thank him.

translation:
Thousands of officials surround the emperor, their belts adorned with jeweled ornaments, while five guards stand in formation on either side. One holds a golden mallet, the other an axe; the two stand in unison.

Red silk candles illuminate the room, incense from a burning brazier fills the air, creating an atmosphere of grandeur. Dragons and phoenixes dance, hawks and eagles soar. The holy sovereign, the enlightened emperor, is present; his loyal ministers are righteous. He surpasses the virtues of Yao and Shun by a thousand years, surpassing the peace of Yu and Tang by ten thousand.

And there, the emperor's staff shines, reflecting the splendor of his dragon-emblazoned robe. Jade rings and a fan decorated with colorful phoenixes radiate auspicious vibes. His jeweled crown, jade belt, purple sash, and gold insignia gleam. A thousand troops of imperial guards surround him, two lines of palanquin bearers follow close behind. The emperor, in a reverent and pious manner, bathes in the light of the Buddha, joyfully accepting the merit of incense offerings.

King Tang arrives early, approaches the temple, commands the musical instruments to be silenced, disembarks from his carriage, and leads his entourage of officials to bow before the Buddha, offering incense.

After three turns, he raises his head to gaze upon the magnificent temple. He sees banners fluttering, jeweled canopies radiating brilliance. The banners flutter and dance, painting the sky with colored clouds; the canopies shine, reflecting the sun's rays like crimson lightning. The Buddha's golden elephant form is truly magnificent, the Arhat's jade faces radiate divine power. 

Flowering immortal blossoms fill the vase, sandalwood incense fills the air.

Immortals blossoms fill the vase, illuminating the magnificent pagoda with their radiance; sandalwood incense fills the air, its fragrance permeates the clear skies. Fresh fruit, artistically arranged on a crimson platter, and unusual sugar pastries stacked on a colorful table are laid out.

High priests chant the true scriptures, hoping to liberate lone souls from suffering. Emperor Taizong, both civil and military, each offers incense, bows before the Buddha's golden statue, and pays homage to the Arhats.

Then, he sees the eminent Master Xuanzang, standing in front of the imperial court, leading the Buddhist monks in prostration before the Tang King.  

After the ceremony, the monks find their respective meditation spots. The master presents Emperor Taizong with a scroll titled "Pardoning the Destitute." The scroll reads: 

"Ultimate virtue is boundless, Zen Buddhism reaches its peak. Pure and illuminating, flowing through the three realms. Changing endlessly, unifying Yin and Yang. Its essence is eternal, infinite. Observing those lost souls, it is essential to show compassion.  Following the Holy Emperor's mandate, I have assembled these monks to practice Zen and preach the Dharma. We open wide the gates of convenience, navigate the vast vessel of compassion, and liberate all beings in the sea of suffering, freeing them from the affliction of the six realms.

Return to the true path, join the boundless cosmic dance; act and cease to act, unifying into pure nothingness. Relying on this good cause, we invite you to admire the celestial court of a clear and beautiful capital; ride this auspicious occasion, escape from the hellish realm of mortals.

Climb to the ultimate bliss freely, roaming the West as you please.

The poem says: 
One furnace of incense for everlasting life, 
Several scrolls of heavenly ascension talismans.

Infinite wonders of the Dharma are proclaimed,
Boundless grace of heaven envelops all. 
All grievances are removed,
All lost souls are released from prison.

May this protect our country, bringing a thousand years of peace and prosperity."

Emperor Taizong, overjoyed, says to the monks:

"You all possess unwavering sincerity, do not neglect Buddhist rituals. When your work is complete and everyone achieves their blessings, I will bestow generous rewards, never letting your efforts go unrewarded."

A thousand two hundred monks, all bow their heads in unison, expressing their gratitude.
